value.text: A man who was released from prison just 11 days ago is back in custody after deputies say he was yelling at people and wandering through a Hobe Sound neighborhood. 28-year-old Joseph Oswald was arrested after residents along the 6000 block of Crooked Oak Avenue called 911 to report the suspicious activity, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office . Deputies responded and found Oswald, who appeared to be under the influence of an unknown substance, the sheriff's office said. See also: Woman with 28 prior felony convictions arrested in Okeechobee drug investigation Oswald has an extensive criminal history, with as many as 14 prior arrests in Martin County on charges ranging from grand theft and burglary to loitering and prowling, according to the sheriff's office. He now faces charges of loitering, prowling, and trespassing. The sheriff's office praised residents for quickly reporting the activity, saying community members play an important role in keeping their neighborhoods safe when they report suspicious behavior.

WPTV has been following flooding on the Treasure Coast caused by strong winds and king tides on Monday.In Martin County, off Dyer Point Road in Palm City, parts of the area were completely underwater.WATCH BELOW: Flooding swamps parts of Palm City amid king tides, strong windsTerresa Baldwin, who lives off the roadway, said it was flooded for a few hours, but water has since retreated."You could smell the sewage; it was really stinky, it was bad," Baldwin said. "There were dead copperheads, so the snakes are coming out. They're getting flushed out with the water."Baldwin said she was also dealing with flooding in her backyard along one of the finger canals.She showed WPTV the water over her dock and in her new patio."The wind was blowing so hard, so it was like waves crashing in your backyard, and you're like, no, nobody wants to see that," Baldwin said.Despite the water going down, she is still worried about what could happen in the next few days."The biggest concern for us is getting water from both sides. What do you do, especially when you're trying to sleep, and you don't know if the water's going to come up more or what's going to get damaged at night when you really can't see," Baldwin said. With high tide later Monday night, the sheriff’s office told WPTV the situation could get worse.Lt. Dave Rosko said they have three high-water vehicles ready for rescue efforts and urged neighbors to think twice before driving through the water."Understand the limitations of your vehicle and do not drive through the high waters," Rosko said. "If your vehicle gets disabled there, it may turn into a rescue event where we need to come out and ensure your safety."Rosko said neighbors living in coastal communities should be aware of future tides before traveling.

Greatness doesn't happen overnight; it takes countless hours and endless repetition.Over the past two years, the girls' flag football team at Seminole Ridge High School has won 37 games and lost only four, while winning two straight championships.WATCH BELOW: Seminole Ridge flag football eyes 3rd straight state title"It's an amazing feeling that the girls are so hungry and into flag football. They love what they do and work so hard. It's really a joy to be the coach," head coach Scott O'Hara said. His joy as a coach comes from having the best team in Florida.The girls are sure-handed, disciplined, and have fun while doing it."If we're too serious with the team, then it's going to be a lot of tension with the team, but adding the jokes and the calmness helps keep the balance between everything," said Samantha Musgrave, the team captain.She knows the girls have a chance to win three straight titles, but takes it day by day."This upcoming season I expect for us to win some games. It's all about who puts in the most work, and I think our team puts in even more work than we need to, for sure," said Musgrave.One reason the girls can let their hair down and be free is thanks to Chachi Saunders, but on the field she's a playmaker.From game-winning catches in the championship to leading the team in almost every statistical category, 17 interceptions last season, and even earning First Team All-Defensive honors.To cap it all off, she's the first flag footballer in Palm Beach County to commit to a Division I school for flag football."I didn't know this would ever happen, but I'm so proud and so happy to have all of my coaches to help me and my team being on my back," said Saunders.

More defense capabilities are being added outside Mar-a-Lago to protect President Donald Trump when he visits his private club.On Monday, WPTV spotted two ground-based air defense assets aboard a barge that was floating in the Intracoastal Waterway outside Mar-a-Lago.WATCH BELOW: Barge with air defense assets spotted outside Mar-a-LagoThese new details come after WPTV reported Friday that NORAD and USNORTHCOM confirmed they deployed assets in and around Mar-a-Lago at the Secret Service's request. It's unclear if a specific threat prompted the deployment of these defense systems. "Due to security considerations, we cannot provide tactics, techniques and procedural specifics," NORAD said in a statement. Also, NORAD said one of its F-16s intercepted a plane that flew into restricted airspace Saturday near Mar-a-Lago."After the fighter jet executed a standard headbutt maneuver to gain the pilot’s attention, the civilian aircraft established communication and safely exited the restricted airspace in full compliance with flight instructions," NORAD said in a statement.According to the military, pilots who violate restricted airspace may also be met by federal authorities upon landing and subject to enforcement action.WPTV reporter Joel Lopez reported this month that fighter pilots have intercepted more than 60 aircraft violating temporary flight restrictions around Palm Beach since January 2025.

A West Palm Beach homeowner says she was locked out of the My Safe Florida Home program while she was in the hospital with a broken hip."I applied for it, and they told me you're doing fine, and then when I got out of the hospital and got here, I called them up, or I texted them, and they said, 'You haven't responded to our emails, so it's over,'" Barbara Madewell said.WATCH BELOW: Woman, 85, says hospital stay cost her $10K home grantShe tells me she had recently completed her second home inspection with the program after replacing windows and a roof before she broke her hip during a fall in early September.The 85-year-old said she spent more than weeks in two hospitals for surgery and then had physical therapy.She was hoping to resume the process with the program to get a $10,000 grant to offset her costs of over $60,000."It's very frustrating to me, very frustrating," she said. I have no income other than my husband's pension and Social Security."The My Safe Florida Home program has helped thousands of homeowners with storm-strengthening repairs to lower insurance costs.In the last two years, the program was changed by lawmakers to prioritize low-income and senior homeowners.The program can take months to complete, and it is also known for strict deadlines, forcing many homeowners to keep close watch on emails and texts.I have reached out to the state Department of Financial Services with information about Madewell's situation.

A proposal that could provide property-tax relief to Florida homeowners is raising concerns among Palm Beach County nonprofit leaders who worry the savings could come with consequences for organizations serving families already struggling to make ends meet.Nearly 100 people gathered in Wellington Monday for a presentation hosted by the Nonprofit Chamber of Palm Beach County focused on the potential community impact of Amendment 3, including what organizers say it could mean for nonprofit funding and local services.WATCH BELOW: Nonprofits raise concerns over Amendment 3A statewide survey by the Florida Nonprofit Alliance found that 92% of nonprofits surveyed said they would face an impact if Amendment 3 passes. Of those surveyed, 65% reported they may have to cut programs or services or turn clients away.Monday's panel featured the following speakers:Leah McDermott, vice president of Policy & Programs at the Florida Nonprofit AllianceFormer Palm Beach County Deputy Administrator Tammy Fields Jennifer Sullivan, senior vice president of the Cultural Council for Palm Beach CountyPastor Rae Whitely of Faith in Florida"The nonprofit chamber is really trying to educate the community about Amendment 3 and its impact specifically on the nonprofit community as it relates to programming that is funded through the county and special taxing districts like Children's Services Council and the Healthcare District," said Michelle Gonzalez, president of the Nonprofit Chamber.Gonzalez said nonprofits across Palm Beach County provide a wide range of services."They're serving pregnant women, children, families, education, childcare, health, you name it. The nonprofit community is doing it, and I don't think people realize the impact on the hundreds of thousands of residents throughout Palm Beach County that are utilizing these services," Gonzalez said.She said the discussion surrounding Amendment 3 is complicated by the potential savings for homeowners."When you look at the property tax valuations, you're talking about $166 on an average home that's about $350,000. So that's how much they would invest in a year in that property tax," Gonzalez said.But Gonzalez said nonprofit organizations rely on funding from several sources, including special taxing districts."It's absolutely crucial. The nonprofit community is working with private funders and individual donors, but we also do rely on special taxing districts like Children's Services Council, like the Healthcare District, to provide services that those entities can't, that the county government cannot," Gonzalez said.She said Children's Services Council could face a significant reduction."When you talk about special taxing districts like Children's Services Council, they're looking at a $25 million reduction in their budget by 2028. And so that's a huge hit to the more than 700 nonprofits that are being funded through them," Gonzalez said.That potential ripple effect was one of the biggest concerns raised during the event.Ruth, who said she is with CROS Ministries, an organization that helps provide people with access to healthy food, said she came to learn how Amendment 3 could affect both nonprofit organizations and the residents walking through their doors."What brought me out here is to hear what the impact of Amendment 3 is on our community and also on the people that we serve, because it's going to affect the funding that's coming to nonprofits, but also, at the end of the day, affect the people that are coming in through our doors," she said.She said one of her biggest takeaways was that the impact could reach beyond homeowners."So one of the things that I learned is the fact that renters are going to be affected, that there's a trickle down, and although some funds, although some agencies may not be getting funding directly from property taxes, it's going to increase the number of people who are coming into our agencies," Ruth said.She described the potential impact as a "circle domino effect.""Yes, it's a circle domino effect that will affect everybody, and I think if we really look at it, even for those of us who may not be affected financially, at the end of the day, our community, we have our brothers, we have our sisters, we have our neighbors. So at the end of the day, what affects one affects all of us," Ruth said.Whiteley, an organizer with Faith in Florida and CEO of Trinity Counseling Center, was one of the panel speakers."Saving money shouldn't come at the cost of somebody else's expense," Whiteley said.He acknowledged that property taxes are a concern but said he does not believe Amendment 3 is the answer."Absolutely. I think that property taxes are definitely a problem and we have to address it. This is just not the way," Whiteley said."We really have to study impact or consequences before we make decisions, and I don't think that we've had a, we haven't had an opportunity to study the consequences or the long-term impact on the state of Florida. This was rushed, so we have to do something. I just don't believe that Amendment 3 is that option because we haven't studied the consequences," he added.Then came a question Whiteley said churches may eventually have to confront."If they can't meet that need, you have people who are already struggling, struggle more, and they always come back to the church. And with the church itself struggling, we, we will have our doors open," he said. "But how long can we sustain it? The collection plate should not be a substitute for a county budget," Whiteley said.Whiteley said some nonprofits are already dealing with financial challenges even before any potential effects from Amendment 3."Yeah, there are nonprofit organizations that we're speaking with that are saying that their budget has already been cut 20 to 30% and they had to make layoffs, right? And that's not post Amendment 3," Whiteley said."When they lose more funding, they will have to decide whether they're gonna keep those doors open, or they're gonna try to find funding in other areas," he added.Trudy Crowetz with Nonprofits First said the gathering brought together organizations working in different areas of the community."So I'm out here to help the nonprofit sector understand the implications of Amendment 3, the property tax amendment, so we are involved with all of our different types of nonprofits, health and human services, arts and culture, family services, education, so we serve every cause, so we want to make sure that our constituents are well informed about the implications of property tax amendment number 3," Crowetz said.She said Palm Beach County's economic diversity is an important part of the conversation."Because I know that Palm Beach County is a very diverse county and so there are, like I mentioned, areas of wealth and pockets of poverty as well so, keeping that in mind we talk about that as a statewide perspective but we also, we need to figure that out as a county how that's going to affect the different areas within our county," Crowetz said.Gonzalez said those economic differences are also why nonprofits are focused on residents who may have jobs but continue to struggle with basic expenses."There's this population called the ALICE population that United Way of Palm Beach County is really pushing forward. It's asset-limited, income-constrained, but employed, and it's this pocket of individuals and families across the community that are working sometimes two and three jobs, but they're still struggling to make ends meet. That's the area, that's the population that we're trying to serve," Gonzalez said.With Election Day approaching, Gonzalez said the chamber's goal is to get information in front of voters who are still making their decision."Very much so. We are trying to do our part in advocating through the nonprofit chamber so that we can really educate the community, those who really haven't made their decision yet on which way they want to vote. That's what today is all about," Gonzalez said.Whiteley said the gathering now needs to translate into greater community involvement."I think today went really well. I think that whenever you have over 100 people in a room sharing a message, that's important, right? Now, how do we move from being attendees to being organizers?" Whiteley said.His final message focused less on organizations and more on the people who make up the community."Stay involved. Think about the impact that it will have on your neighbor, and let's start thinking more as a collective and not individually," Whiteley said.In Florida, all constitutional amendments require a 60% vote to be approved.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Plans to bring a Buc-ee's travel center to the Treasure Coast are continuing to move forward.During questioning from a St. Lucie County commissioner last week, county Planning Director Ben Balser said Buc-ee's has received site plan approval and its building permits are currently under review.Balser said the county is ready to move forward once Buc-ee's addresses the remaining comments from county staff.Plans for the travel center were first announced in 2023. The project calls for a 120-pump location off Indrio Road off Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County.Buc-ee's website continues to list the location as opening in 2027.The Texas-based travel center chain is known for its large stores and expansive fueling areas. Lucie County location would bring the popular chain to the Treasure Coast.

The race to be Florida's next governor is a competitive one — a statistical tie, according to a poll released last week by the University of North Florida.I caught up with Republican Byron Donalds and Democrat David Jolly as they each campaigned across the state, pitching different visions of Florida's future to voters.WATCH BELOW: Donalds, Jolly pitch competing visions in tight governor's raceDonalds, a Republican congressman, told me in a video call from his campaign bus on the road that he wants to build on the policies he likes from Gov. Ron DeSantis' outgoing administration."We live in a great state, and what has separated us from the other states is we continue to choose common sense conservative policy," Donalds said.That includes immigration enforcement."We're going to continue that mission here in the great state of Florida because we are going to continue to follow the law. I think that's the appropriate use of state authority and state powers," Donalds said.It also includes Florida's Department of Government Efficiency, which DeSantis formed through an executive order in 2025 and has since conducted audits of multiple counties across Florida."We are going to DOGE all governments, both local and state agencies in the state of Florida, because it's not our tax money. It belongs to the people of Florida. We need to make sure that government lives within its means, the way families have to live within their means," Donalds said.Donalds told me that effort will be important if Amendment 3 passes, raising homestead tax exemptions and reducing local revenue. I asked him whether, as governor, he would be prepared if some of the municipalities that need help come to Tallahassee asking for it."Yes, we will, and we've already made a public commitment to the fiscally constrained counties in the state of Florida," Donalds said. "Those that we know that their budgets are going to change in a major way, that we're prepared to provide a funding formula for those fiscally constrained counties so that they can be able to make ends meet."Jolly, a Democrat who served as a Republican in Congress during the 2010s, visited WPTV as his campaign traveled through Palm Beach County. He has said he personally opposes Amendment 3, but will support the will of the voters if it passes."I think we all want the math behind Amendment 3 to work, but it just doesn't," Jolly said.Florida hasn't elected a Democrat as governor since the 1990s. I asked Jolly why he thinks that is and why he believes his campaign could overcome that."Look, we're a state that trended Republican, particularly in the last eight years, and we know by voter registration it's still a predominantly Republican state," Jolly said. "I think we're in a moment most akin to a 1974 post-Watergate moment, where voters are saying, 'Burn the ships. Let's go in a new direction.'"Jolly said that direction should be simple."Housing, healthcare, education, and no data centers. "The answers are not in ideology. The answers are in solutions."He also said he wants to reach across the aisle to achieve those goals."If we expand health care access, we reduce costs. So you can be a conservative that wants to save money or a progressive that wants more health care. When we invest in public education, we create a resilient economy that should be attractive to Republicans. The economic argument behind that, I think, on housing, when more people have stable housing, the economy is better. I think we can work with Republicans," Jolly said.One issue where the two candidates agree is on school choice. Both told me they support keeping universal vouchers in place.Jolly also emphasized his desire to increase transparency requirements in Florida's charter schools and increase teacher pay in public schools."Let's engage in a little bit of consumer protection here on behalf of kids and families, and say that if you're going to take a voucher as a school, you should have to provide the same services, standards and offerings and be measured by the same measuring stick that our public schools are," Jolly said.Asked whether financial records of charter schools should be public records, as they are for public schools, Donalds replied, "I think if you're talking about what parents are looking for, what they want to basically see, are the children being educated? What are the mathematical attainment scores of that school? What are the reading attainment scores of that school? And if you're talking about high school, what's the ACT scores and what's the SAT scores? I think that's the accountability and the transparency that parents are looking for in the state of Florida, because at the end of the day, they're looking to make sure that the output is where it needs to be."Donalds' wife, Erika Donalds, founded a charter school company and currently runs a nonprofit promoting school choice. "My wife is actually not in the charter school business anymore. She's actually been out of that business for a couple of years," Donalds told me. "But I just want to be clear: she will not be contracting with the state of Florida in any way, shape, or form."On data center policy, the candidates differ. Jolly said he supports a moratorium on data center construction, while Donalds believes those decisions should be left up to local governments."If a local government says no data centers, then no data centers. If they do, then where the state steps in is we make sure that utility bills, utility costs are not passed on to consumers, and we also make sure that we are going to protect water resources in our state," Donalds said.For the first time in decades, Florida voters did not get to see a gubernatorial debate for this election.Asked what he would say to Jolly had the two candidates faced one another on the debate stage, Donalds said, "I would like him to explain why and how the people of Florida are going to be able to pay for his insurance plan, because by independent analysis, his insurance plan will drive up premiums on the people of our state, and everybody will be hit with a $1,000 hurricane tax when the next time the big storm comes through," referring to the funding the sovereign wealth fund Jolly says he would like to create to cover windstorm damage for Florida homeowners. (Jolly has denied that the fund would impose a new tax.)"I'm not sure debates improve our politics at this point. I think they just platform the division and the vitriol and the ugliness," Jolly told me. "My wife says in a world of Donald Trump, I'm trying to be Ted Lasso. We have two young kids, and I want them to look back and know that Dad acted in a way that he spoke of, which was not to further devolve our politics into vitriol and ugliness and division. Debates are about who can score the greatest insult, and I just I don't think that helps."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Nearly half a million USAA auto insurance policies in Florida are set to see lower rates after state regulators approved a series of reductions, according to the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation.Florida Insurance Commissioner Mike Yaworsky approved several auto insurance program rate decreases for USAA Group that average 7%. The changes affect more than 498,000 policies across the state.Individual policyholders could see different savings depending on their program. According to the state, average rate changes range from a decrease of 0.4% to as much as 11.2%.USAA has its highest concentration of Florida business in Brevard, Escambia and Okaloosa counties. Average decreases in those counties are 5.8% in Brevard, 8% in Escambia and 8.4% in Okaloosa."The Office of Insurance Regulation is constantly reaching out to insurers to inquire about rate relief, and USAA is always stepping up to the plate and looking out for their consumers," Yaworsky said in the release.He encouraged other insurers to consider additional rate reductions.Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia pointed to the reductions as another sign of improvement in the state's insurance market and credited Florida's tort reforms."These auto insurance rate decreases will help Florida families keep more of their hard-earned money in their pockets, especially our military families," Ingoglia said.The latest reductions follow other savings announced by USAA over the past year. According to the release, the company provided nearly $1 billion in rate reductions and direct member returns to Florida members between December 2025 and July 2026. That included a $500 million dividend distributed to approximately 830,000 members.State regulators also said Florida's five largest auto insurance groups are showing a combined indicated rate change of negative 12.6% for 2026. Those companies represent 81% of Florida's auto insurance market, according to the release.The state also reported that Florida had the nation's lowest personal auto liability loss ratio in 2025 at 52.5%, its lowest level in 15 years.

A panel of federal appellate judges on Sunday questioned the timing, constitutionality and authority of the Justice Department's demand that California election officials set aside thousands of mail ballots from people the federal government suspects may not be citizens.During rare weekend arguments, two of the three judges on the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals appeared skeptical of a lawsuit brought by President Donald Trump's administration in mid-October. The lawsuit accuses California officials of failing to meet a 48-hour deadline to review 20,000 names the administration flagged as likely noncitizens on the state's voter rolls.The administration asked a federal judge to require the state to withhold counting those ballots until the voters’ immigration status could be verified. The district judge scheduled a hearing for Oct. 27, days after the case was assigned, but the federal government appealed to the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, seeking an expedited decision.Justice Department attorney Matthew Donnelly told the panel that California is causing irreparable harm “by allowing noncitizens to vote in violation of their own state laws. The damage is irreversible and irrevocable.”RELATED STORY | DOJ threatens California with legal action over claim of noncitizens on voter rollsThe Trump administration has made efforts to identify noncitizen voters a priority this year, even though noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare.Circuit Judge Mark Bennett, a Trump appointee, questioned whether the appellate court even has jurisdiction to hear the case even before a ruling by the lower court.Donnelly argued that the schedule set by the lower court judge was too slow and effectively a denial of the government's request, as state elections officials process thousands of mail ballots every day.Judge Gabriel Sanchez, appointed by former President Joe Biden, questioned whether the federal government was violating the Tenth Amendment, essentially commandeering the state to enforce a federal law that makes it a misdemeanor for a noncitizen to vote.The federal government is simply asking California to enforce their own law, which also bans noncitizens from voting, Donnelly said. He argued the state's refusal to comply with the federal request to set aside the ballots for review was “frustrating the purpose” of the federal law against noncitizen voting.The Elections Clause of the U.S. Constitution gives state legislatures the power to set the time, place and manner of congressional elections, Bennett said. The executive branch may be “unhappy with what they’re doing, and doesn’t like the manner,” Bennett said, but under the Election Clause the state has the right to determine those issues — including how it sorts out any noncitizen voters.Attorney Seth Waxman, representing Los Angeles County Clerk Dean Logan, said the federal government's list was unreliable and that segregating the ballots for a review process would effectively disenfranchise thousands of eligible voters.Even if election staffers spent just three minutes checking each of the expected 2.75 million mail ballots against the government's list, the process would take 140,000 man-hours, Waxman said — or about 16 years of working time.Waxman cited a review of 200 records from the Trump administration's list conducted by Los Angeles County staffers. Assistant Registrar-Recorder Monica Flores said in a court filing that the sample included canceled or inactive registrations, individuals with no voting history and voters who appeared to have been born in the United States, which the filing notes “is strong evidence of citizenship.”If the administration disagrees with how California runs its elections, it can ask Congress to change that process, said attorney Sam Siegel, representing California Secretary of State Shirley Weber.The federal government has provided no credible evidence to support its suspicions, said Siegal.“It has no basis in law or in fact,” he told the panel. “We just dispute the premise that noncitizens are voting."But Judge Patrick Bumatay, who was appointed by Trump, said everyone has an interest in ensuring that only eligible citizens vote. He suggested that granting the administration's request for an emergency order could provide clarity.“Without an injunction, you will never know” if that is happening, Bumatay told Seigel.Bennett said the panel would try to issue a ruling as quickly as possible.

A 23-year-old Road Ranger from West Palm Beach was killed early Sunday after a driver entered a lane closure at an Interstate 95 crash investigation scene and struck him before hitting a Florida Highway Patrol cruiser, according to FHP.The crash happened around 2:07 a.m. on northbound I-95 near Lantana Road in Palm Beach County.WATCH REPORT BELOW: According to FHP, a 2019 Mercedes sedan driven by an 18-year-old Lake Worth woman was traveling north in the inside center lane.At the time, a marked FHP Dodge Charger was stationary across the inside and inside center lanes with its emergency lights activated as part of a lane closure for an ongoing crash investigation.Investigators said the Mercedes entered the closed lane and struck the 23-year-old Road Ranger. The car then rotated and collided with the FHP cruiser.The man was pronounced dead at the scene. His identity has not been released.The 18-year-old driver suffered non-incapacitating injuries and was taken to JFK South for treatment.The outside northbound lane of I-95 reopened at 8:34 a.m., according to FHP.The name of the Road Ranger who was killed has not been released.

LagoonFest returns to the downtown West Palm Beach waterfront Saturday with free boat tours, wildlife encounters, children's activities and opportunities to learn about the Lake Worth Lagoon.The free festival runs from 8:30 a.m. near the West Palm Beach GreenMarket. Benji Studt of Palm Beach County Environmental Resources Management said the event is designed to help residents and visitors connect with the lagoon."It's all about connecting people with the lagoon," Studt said.Visitors can explore the Lake Worth Lagoon aboard the Hakuna Matata or through Aqua Adventure tours, according to Studt.The boat tours provide a chance to experience the lagoon from the water while learning more about the natural area and the work being done around it.Studt said participating organizations include the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, Busch Wildlife Sanctuary and Manatee Lagoon.The festival will feature touch tanks, wildlife experiences and a live python capture demonstration from FWC.Throughout the morning, families can also meet Laguna, the spotted eagle ray mascot representing Lake Worth Lagoon.Studt said this year's children's zone includes a shell hunt, giveaways and calendars featuring work from local artists.Volunteers from the West Palm Beach Fishing Foundation will teach children how to cast and fish. Participating children will also get to take home a rod and reel, according to Studt."The kids can come, and they can do a little shell hunt, look for their shell treasures," Studt said.LagoonFest gives South Florida families a free way to spend time together while learning about a waterway that is part of Palm Beach County's environmental identity.Its location also allows visitors to pair the festival with a stop at the nearby West Palm Beach GreenMarket. Studt said the variety of activities makes the event accessible to visitors with different interests."There's something for everybody at LagoonFest," Studt said. "It's going to be an awesome time."LagoonFest takes place Saturday from 8:30 a.m. along the downtown West Palm Beach waterfront.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic died while on duty Saturday, more than a year after his younger brother, who also served as a firefighter-paramedic, died at age 26. Lucie County Fire District announced the line-of-duty death of Austin Hodge on Saturday, Oct. 24, calling his death a profound loss to the department and the fire service community. Hodge joined the district on July 17, 2017, and served the community for more than nine years. He was assigned to Station 9. Neighboring Indian River County Fire Rescue also shared condolences following the firefighter’s unexpected death Saturday morning. Lucie County Fire District asked the public to respect Hodge’s family as they grieve. Information about memorial arrangements will be shared as details are finalized. Read more: Missing 5-year-old girl found dead in Fort Pierce body of water Brothers shared a career in firefighting Austin Hodge’s death comes more than a year after his younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic, died on July 22, 2025. The brothers shared a close bond and a passion for serving their community. This was my best friend, my twin, Austin Hodge previously told CBS12 News. We had the same hairstyle. He described Jarius as someone who loved his family and his work as a first responder. He loved going to work, loved working beside me. I loved working beside him, Austin said. He always pushed me to keep going. He was someone who loved his family, his community and his country. Family sought accountability after Jarius’ death In an interview with CBS12 News , Austin said Jarius became ill after catching the flu from a patient at work in July 2025. Austin said his younger brother went to Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie on July 22, struggling to breathe, but died hours later. He alleged that medical staff made critical errors in treating his brother, including taking three attempts to intubate him. He said Jarius had been healthy before becoming ill. Austin also spoke publicly about Florida’s medical malpractice laws, arguing that restrictions on who can pursue certain wrongful-death claims prevented his family from seeking legal accountability for Jarius’ death. This is unjust, and it's been going on for too long, Austin said in the earlier interview. He emphasized that his family was seeking accountability rather than financial compensation. For me personally, for my family, this has nothing to do with any type of dollar, he said. We just want those physicians to be held accountable. The circumstances surrounding Austin Hodge’s death have not been released. Lucie County Fire District said additional information about ways to honor his service will be shared in coordination with his family.

A 5-year-old nonverbal girl was located deceased in a body of water near her home in Fort Pierce three hours after she was reported missing, police said Saturday afternoon. The Fort Pierce Police Department was looking for Mayra Glory Odelus, who was last seen in the 5100 block of Portofino Landing Apartments east of Interstate 95 before noon. A diving team was utilized to search for her. "Our deepest condolences are with Mayra’s family and loved ones during this tragic time," the agency posted in an update at 4:15 p.m. Michael Santiago told WPBF's Angela Rozier they received the report of the missing girl at 11:39 a.m., with family members saying she was autistic and nonverbal. Officers searched the surrounding area and distributed flyers with the girl's name and photo. She was last seen wearing a dark oversized shirt with two white beads in her hair, the agency said. They also launched drones, and requested assistance from Port St. Lucie bloodhounds and the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office dive team. The child's body was found in the pond at about 3 p.m. about 75 yards from hert apartment. Police said the child's father told them the pond is directly across from their apartment and she loved the water. The father and her 18-year-old sister were home at the time the girl went missing. If you're traveling for Thanksgiving, one question could significantly affect your holiday budget: Is it cheaper to fly or drive?The answer can depend on where you're going, how many people are traveling, and when you plan to leave and return.Travelers we spoke with were divided.WATCH: Is it cheaper to fly or drive this Thanksgiving?"It depends where you're going," Leticia Rivera said. "But I would say fly right now."Others would rather stay on the road."For the preference, regardless of pricing, drive," Erik Eliassen said."Oh, definitely drive," Calvin Landau added.Carol Baxter, meanwhile, has already made her decision: "I'm flying."According to Hopper data provided for this story, the average domestic round-trip flight for Thanksgiving is currently about $402 per person, compared with $307 last year.For a family of four, four tickets at the $402 average would total about $1,608 in airfare alone, before adding other potential travel expenses.Driving can look very different because everyone in the vehicle shares expenses such as fuel. Using the example in our comparison, the driving cost is about $160.That means families should consider the total cost of the trip rather than simply comparing the price of one plane ticket with one tank of gas.For people planning to fly, choosing a different return date could also affect the cost.Hopper data provided for this story shows a round trip with a return on the Sunday after Thanksgiving averaging about $604.Returning on Monday or Tuesday, however, could bring that average down to around $350.That's a difference of roughly $254 per ticket.For a family of four, that difference could potentially add up to more than $1,000.There isn't one answer that works for every Thanksgiving traveler.Flying may save time on a long-distance trip, while driving can make the cost easier to spread across several people traveling together.Before booking, compare the total cost for everyone traveling, including airfare or fuel and any additional expenses associated with the trip. Also consider whether changing your travel dates could bring down the price.For families in particular, doing the math on the entire trip could make a significant difference in the Thanksgiving travel budget.

The Village of Indiantown is moving forward with plans to consider a temporary moratorium on large-scale data center development, but three sites already in the works would be excluded from the proposed restrictions. During Thursday night's Village Council meeting, members voted to schedule a special meeting for November 5, when they will take up the first reading of an ordinance that would temporarily halt new data center development applications, reviews, approvals and the start of construction on projects subject to the restrictions. The council also identified three sites that would be excluded from the proposed moratorium: Project Silver Fox Associated with Silver Fox 606 LLC. Project Growler Associated with Warfield 18 LLC. Tesoro Groves A large, planned development associated with Florida Power & Light property. The exemptions would allow those sites to remain outside the proposed restrictions while the village considers how to regulate future large-scale data center development. Council seeks negotiations and an end to litigation Council members also called for lawsuits surrounding the developments to be dropped as the village seeks to negotiate with developers. The request comes amid ongoing legal disputes involving data center development in Indiantown. Silver Fox 606 LLC filed a lawsuit against the village challenging its handling of an appeal involving the project's development approvals. A Martin County circuit judge issued an injunction earlier this month blocking a planned zoning appeals hearing while the legal dispute proceeds. It remains unclear whether the developers will agree to dismiss pending litigation or what conditions could be attached to any negotiations. Councilwoman pushes for community benefits See also: Palm Beach County district says 12 K-8 schools made Florida’s top 100 in new rankings During Thursday's meeting, Councilwoman Vernestine Williams-Palmer expressed frustration over the lengthy discussions surrounding data centers and emphasized the need to secure financial benefits for Indiantown residents. Palmer said the village needs additional tax revenue and investments in community infrastructure, particularly improvements to its water system. We need all the things, all the things that's been promised. We need the community impacts. We need all of that," Palmer said, according to a transcript of the meeting. She also encouraged residents to identify improvements they would like developers to help fund, mentioning a proposed $3 million gymnasium as one example discussed. Palmer said she has visited a data center in Texas and spoken with facility managers as part of her efforts to better understand the industry. While acknowledging that residents remain divided over data center development, Palmer said council members are working to protect the community's interests. The November 5 special meeting will focus on the first reading of the proposed moratorium ordinance. If ultimately adopted, the measure would temporarily restrict new large-scale data center applications and development activity covered by the ordinance while excluding the three identified sites. The length of the proposed moratorium and the precise conditions governing the exemptions still need to be established. The council's October 22 vote scheduled the special meeting and addressed the proposed exclusions. It did not enact the moratorium. Village leaders are expected to continue discussions over development restrictions, infrastructure needs and potential community benefits as the ordinance moves forward.

Lucie County Fire District firefighter who died unexpectedly Saturday morning has been identified as Austin Hodge, a firefighter paramedic and nine-year veteran of the department. The fire district announced Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk during a shift change. He was taken to the hospital and passed away. Lucie County firefighter dies on duty "Today, our St. Lucie County Fire District family mourns the loss of one of our own," the district said in a statement. In the hours following his death, firefighters, the department's Honor Guard and fellow first responders gathered to honor Hodge and support one another. The district said the response reflected the strong bond shared throughout the fire service. The district thanked the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Fort Pierce Police Department, Port St. Lucie Police Department and peer support teams from Martin and Indian River counties for providing assistance and standing alongside firefighters during the difficult day. "Together, they offered strength, compassion, and support while ensuring Austin was honored with the dignity and respect he deserves," the district said. The district said its thoughts are with Hodge's family, loved ones and everyone who served alongside him. They respectfully ask that Hodge's family be given privacy during this time. "We are deeply grateful to our fellow first responders and community for the outpouring of support during this tremendous loss," the district said. "Today and always, we stand together." The tragedy comes more than a year after the community mourned the sudden loss of his brother, Jarius Hodge , 26, who was also a St. Lucie County firefighter and died from septic shock in July 2025. The district said it will share information on funeral and memorial services in coordination with the family when it becomes available.

Civil rights advocates are investigating what they call abusive conditions inside a state-run immigration detention facility, telling me they've received a surge of complaints after the Everglades detention camp known as "Alligator Alcatraz" closed over the summer.When Alligator Alcatraz shut down over the summer, it didn't end Florida's involvement in immigration detention. There's a second state-run facility that's been open for a year — in a former prison about 50 minutes west of Jacksonville. Because its location is less controversial than the Everglades, it's flown largely under the radar. But now, detainees are speaking up about the alleged horrors inside what state officials have dubbed "Deportation Depot.""It's insane. There's no other word [to describe the situation] than insanity. Just how bad these conditions were," said a man who asked that we hide his face and refer to him by his middle name, Ryan.He fears being publicly identified could jeopardize his still-pending immigration case."I'm happy to be here, and I'm grateful, and obviously I'm gonna do everything I can to complete my immigration journey, and hopefully I can put this behind me," Ryan said.I learned from the American Civil Liberties Union and confirmed through federal court records and local news reports that Ryan was detained by immigration authorities in late February and sent to the Baker Correctional Institution in Sanderson, where he spent four months. According to the most recent ICE detention data from July, roughly a thousand migrant men are housed at Baker. The ACLU put the number even higher, at about 1,200, during Ryan's stay."They were businessmen, entrepreneurs, paramedics, people that had been in the military. It was just, it was just everyone," Ryan said.Ryan told me about 100 people in his dorm, with four working toilets and four working showers.He described the bathrooms as filthy, toiletries as scarce, and extreme heat as a persistent problem."We had one small AC unit in the corner of the room, which didn't work because the windows were smashed open anyway and kind of had been left broken," Ryan said. "We had black mold, brown mold. Like I said, those infestations of creatures. We had spiders, fire ants, cockroaches, bugs of all description."On Oct. 8, the ACLU, Southern Poverty Law Center and Americans for Immigrant Justice sent a demand letter decrying the alleged conditions inside Baker to the state of Florida, the federal government, and the private contractors that operate the facility.The letter describes conditions matching Ryan's account. The facility was closed as a correctional complex five years ago and sat empty until it reopened for immigration detention in 2025. The letter said it never had proper air conditioning, noting that the lack of adequate cooling results in temperatures of 98 degrees or higher during the daytime in the summer — well above the 88-degree threshold that significantly increases the risk of illness and death. Read full letter:Ryan blames the squalor for the illness and infections he says swept through the detention center."I very quickly started to get ill, and I'm normally not going to get sick very easily. I'm very active," Ryan said.He told me he developed multiple infections on his feet and fungal infections in both ears."I'm a 29-year-old man, and I fainted and passed out for the first time ever in my life in this facility," Ryan said. "I just remember waking up on the floor and people surrounding me, and they're banging on the window trying to get the guard's attention."Ryan told me doctors at a nearby hospital diagnosed him with an enlarged heart. I was not able to independently confirm Ryan's diagnosis, as Ryan claims guards took his medical paperwork and never returned it to him. Here's what Ryan claimed a medical employee told him when he got back to Baker:"Oh yeah, here's a basic painkiller and a bottle of water. If you have any more issues, feel free to put in a sick request, and we'll get round to you when we see you," Ryan said.The letter details an account matching Ryan's experience:"In another disturbing example, a 29-year-old reported that after being detained at BCI for about a month, he passed out one morning and fell to the ground. When he awoke, other detained people told him that he had been unconscious for six or seven minutes, and that no Facility staff made any effort to check on him during that time. Two other detained people, former paramedics, ran over to help him, while GEO Officers just yelled at him for ruining their morning. Shortly after fainting, he developed significant chest pain, and GEO Officers only agreed to call an ambulance after he and other detained people pleaded for help. At the emergency room, doctors ran numerous tests and diagnosed him with an enlarged heart. They told him that he needed to carefully monitor his stress levels and blood pressure. The BCI officers took his hospital medical records, which he never received. When he returned to BCI, he verbally relayed the hospital’s report to the CDR Health nurse, an APRN, who advised him that they were not worried about his heart and that his condition was simply caused by dehydration. The nurse documented “dehydration” as the cause of his fainting episode in his BCI medical records, despite the hospital’s tests and the doctor’s diagnosis."Medical neglect is just one of several allegations Ryan made that are also detailed in the 21-page demand letter. The advocacy groups wrote that they have conducted dozens of interviews with people currently or recently detained at the facility, their loved ones, and attorneys representing people detained there, and that those interviews confirm the widespread abuses occurring there.The letter identifies seven categories of abuse: life-threatening medical neglect; lack of adequate food and clean drinking water; excessive, life-threatening heat; squalid, unsanitary, and unsafe living conditions; deprivation of necessities for physical, mental, and emotional wellbeing, such as sleep, family visitation, and outdoor recreation; verbal and physical abuse and retaliation; and lack of access to the courts and to confidential communications with attorneys.On food and water, the letter alleges that the facility fails to provide people detained there with enough nutritious food, with detained people reporting receiving only "extremely small, infant-sized food portions that are not filling" and lacking adequate protein or nutrients. It states that people are losing dangerous amounts of weight, citing examples including one person who lost 29 pounds in less than two months and another who lost 44 pounds over seven months. On water, it alleges that the facility is failing to provide adequate access to clean drinking water, that most of the time the only drinking water available is from the dorms' visibly rusty water fountains, and that newly detained people are quickly warned not to drink from those fountains because many have gotten sick from drinking that water.Ryan said he and other detainees often spent part of their brief mealtimes drinking as much water as they could from the cafeteria, which he said provided clean drinking water."You had no alternative sometimes than just to kind of take your chances with the water (in the dorm)," Ryan said. "It had a very strong metallic taste, and as soon as it settled in your stomach, it felt like something was kicking and punching your stomach.""It's very much a cruel facility that's designed to deny people every aspect of humanity and decency and dignity, and is designed to make people physically weak, mentally weak, and just pressured to agree to the point— where they agree to self deportation," said ACLU attorney Amy Godshall, who wrote the letter.The letter alleges that this pressure is deliberate, stating there is evidence of a deliberate effort to make immigration detention unbearable so that people abandon their rights and accept departure or removal, and that whether intentional or not, these abusive living conditions are punitive and unconstitutional. Ryan told me he was pulled aside on three or four occasions by guards and asked to sign forms consenting to his deportation."The question that a lot of us had is, well, if we were deportable, then why would we have to sign this document to make us deportable?" Ryan said.I sent detailed questions about the allegations to the Florida Division of Emergency Management, ICE and the Department of Homeland Security, and all three private contractors named in the letter. FDEM and two of the three contractors did not respond. The Boca Raton-based GEO Group declined comment and referred me back to FDEM, even though my questions to them pointed to specific allegations from the letter that their employees pepper-sprayed, isolated, and verbally abused detainees.“The ACLU should just change its name. It’s clear they only care about illegal aliens—not Americans," an ICE spokesperson said in response to my questions.The spokesperson noted that “Baker Correctional Institution is a state-run facility," but said, “Another day and there’s more blatantly FALSE claims that illegal aliens in ICE detention are mistreated, underfed, and not provided adequate medical care.""Ensuring the safety, security, and well-being of individuals in our custody is a top priority at ICE," the ICE spokesperson said. "Being in detention is a choice. We encourage all illegal aliens to take control of their departure with the CBP Home App. The United States is offering illegal aliens $3,000 and a free flight to self-deport now."The ACLU's letter demands that if the facility does not comply with 2026 ICE National Detention Standards and the Constitution, "ICE should immediately end its use of Baker as an immigration detention facility."When I asked Godshall whether she thought she was asking for a lot, she replied: "I don't think we're asking for enough here."As for Ryan, he still doesn't know what secured his release in July."The guy sat me down. I'll never forget what he said. He goes, 'Oh, congratulations, man! You beat us.' I'm like, 'What?'" Ryan said. "It felt like I was part of some kind of weird game show where, at the end of it all, they're going to come out and say, 'Surprise! We got you!' You know, because it was horrific."Ryan said his health has improved since he's gotten out of detention; he hasn't had any infections or cardiac issues, he's put weight back on, and the color returned to his hair after he says it began to gray at Baker. He's now keeping a low public profile until his immigration case is settled."It's just a giant stress and it's just I don't know realistically I don't know how I can prevent that, other than just you know seeing my immigration journey through," Ryan said. Ryan said he finds comfort and support in his friends and in his church."When I pray, I think about the people that are still in there."

For Lantana resident Mitch Freling, heavy rain or a high tide can mean waiting days for the water outside his condo to disappear.“It rains, but when it rains, it floods, and this is what we end up with for a week until it goes away, just evaporates,” Freling said.Freling lives near the Intracoastal Waterway, just north of the Ocean Avenue Bridge. He reached out to WPTV after years of dealing with flooding near his building, saying he wants the Town of Lantana to take another look at drainage in the area.“High tide comes up, it floods this whole area and like, this morning it was up to the wall, but even when it's not high tide, the storm water comes out,” Freling said. “I mean, and it comes down here and fills it up the same way, but there's no way for it to get out.”Freling said he has lived there for 16 years and believes the flooding has gotten worse.Recent high water has him particularly concerned.“This is the highest I've ever seen it. I gotta tell you, I mean, it went over the top of our dock,” Freling said.He worries that if the water gets much higher, it could eventually reach first-floor units.“Look at all the debris up against their front door, and if it gets any higher, it's going in,” he said.Freling said he has previously asked Lantana to address the drainage near his building but was told it was on private property.“I'd like them to at least fix this so it drains,” Freling said.He turned to WPTV hoping to get another set of eyes on the problem."Please help no one is listening," said Freling in his email.“I've reached out to Lantana before and they said that it's our problem,” Freling said. “So I just wanted to reach out to say, hey, you know, there's a problem here. You guys need to address it somehow. You gotta just look at it.”Lantana mayor says town will look into complaintWPTV took Freling's concerns to Lantana Mayor Karen Lythgoe.Lythgoe said Freling's specific complaint was new to her, but she pledged to have the town look into it.However, she cautioned that responsibility could depend on whether the drainage problem is on private property.“If it's a private drainage issue, all we can do is make sure that the public stuff is working as designed,” Lythgoe said.When asked what she would say directly to residents concerned about the flooding, she added, “I'd say to the residents, we'll definitely look into it, but I don't know what the situation is.”The problem is part of a larger challenge facing the coastal community.She said drainage systems designed years ago may no longer have the capacity communities need today.“When you put in a drainage system, you scope it for a certain capacity,” Lythgoe said. “And then as capacity changes, you may not have the capacity that you thought you had in 2011 when you put in the system that you need now. So there's things all constantly need upkeep and maintenance.”Town says drainage and resiliency projects are underwayWPTV previously reported on flooding concerns in Lantana two years ago, when town officials were considering drainage improvements and a fee to help pay for stormwater and other capital projects.Lythgoe said that stormwater utility has since been implemented.The mayor said there are several projects underway, including raising the seawall at Bicentennial Park and a drainage project on Hypoluxo Island.The work can be expensive and require multiple phases, she said, adding that the town is also pursuing Florida resiliency grants and state and federal funding.“Those projects are underway,” Lythgoe said.And the flooding is not limited to the area outside Freling's building. Lythgoe described seeing high water elsewhere around Lantana during the king tide.“This whole parking lot was underwater when I came by to go to the Dune Deck for breakfast. The beach parking lot was underwater, and so was portions of Hypoluxo Island,” she said.But she said some of that water later drained away.For Lythgoe, the bigger question may be whether the town's existing infrastructure needs to be updated for the conditions Lantana is now experiencing.“The infrastructure is working as designed,” Lythgoe said. “So do we need to change that design? I think we do.”She acknowledged the work is far from finished.“There's always more to be done,” Lythgoe said.That's exactly what Freling hopes will happen outside his home.“I'd like them to at least fix this so it drains,” he said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

A young man from the Midwest with South Florida roots describes how Andrew Burnette moved from Michigan around the age of 12 and found home on the football field in Martin County."I played football my whole life, and I can say football is a little harder in Florida than it is in Michigan," said Burnette.WATCH BELOW: Local football standout gets one more shot at college footballWhile football was his first sport, during his high school days at Jensen Beach High School, he fell in love with takedowns and pins."I wasn't zoned for that school, but I went there for wrestling originally; that was my first passion," said Burnette.While he was doing well in wrestling, football kept calling to him."Moving through high school, I knew football was what I wanted to do," said Burnette.He established himself as a force at Jensen Beach High School, but he didn't receive much interest from college football programs, similar to many Treasure Coast football recruits."One of my main struggles was recruitment out of high school, because I felt like our area was a little under-recruited," said Burnette.Betting on himself, he decided to play at Highland Community College in Kansas.Burnette played in nine games and rushed for 340 yards and two touchdowns, but he still wasn't on any other college football program's radar."I transferred to Independence Junior College, and I was cut from the team," said Burnette.Independence was featured on the hit Netflix show Last Chance U, but once his chance there was short-lived, he reached out to Keiser University in West Palm Beach."I spoke with the coach there and told him, 'You guys offered me in high school,' and he said, 'I don't really remember. Send me your film.' He saw my film and said, 'Hey, bring it,'" said Burnette.And he did "bring it." In the two years he played at Keiser, he rushed for over 2,300 yards and 30 touchdowns.With stats like that, Division I programs finally came calling, starting with Louisiana Tech."Last year I played there; it was my first year at the Division I level, and then my eligibility ran out," said Burnette.At the time, the NCAA granted student-athletes only four years of eligibility unless they were injured, so Burnette rolled up his sleeves and got to work."I called my dad and told him, 'Hey, I need to do something. I can't just sit here,' so I went and worked with my dad in Michigan," said Burnette.He worked with his dad at a steel mill in Detroit for a few months, but this summer the NCAA announced the 5-in-5 rule, meaning student-athletes can compete for up to five seasons across a continuous five-year period.So he hired a lawyer and went to court with the NCAA to get his final year of eligibility, and they granted him one last year, and now he's making the most of it."It was amazing; I would rather play football than do anything, and for me to have this opportunity again, it's a blessing," said Burnette.

Jeff Hafley had a towel draped around his neck as he stepped to the podium and the Miami Dolphins coach wiped his face one last time before taking questions from reporters.He had just been doused by his players in the middle of a jubilant locker room after they held on for a 28-25 victory — his first leading the Dolphins — over the New York Jets on Sunday."I grabbed every guy as they ran in," a happy Hafley said. I had so much water on me. It was a really, really special moment, one that I'm appreciative of and one that I won't forget. It was fun."They deserve it. You could feel a lot come out of it. I'm very happy for the players. They did a great job."Malik Willis threw two touchdown passes and ran for a score, and made a victory-sealing 2-yard push up the middle on fourth-and-1 as the Dolphins (1-5) came off their bye-week break and avoided their first 0-6 start since 2019."It was awesome," said Willis, who was 14 of 21 for 208 yards and two TD passes to rookie Caleb Douglas. He also ran for 37 yards on eight carries, but the last one was the biggest of the game.The Jets (2-5) made a late push trailing 28-17. On fourth-and-4, Geno Smith completed a short pass to Isaiah Davis, who zipped downfield 41 yards to the Dolphins' 18. Three plays later, Smith found Mason Taylor for a 12-yard touchdown, the tight end's second of the game.Penalties negated New York's first two 2-point tries before Smith threw to Taylor to make it 28-25 with 3:24 left.Looking to end it, the Dolphins faced fourth-and-1 from the Jets 49 at the two-minute warning, and Hafley went straight to his offensive linemen."I asked them what they thought," Hafley said. "When I saw the look in their eyes, I was very confident that we'd get it. As soon as I saw that, there was no doubt in my mind that we'd go for it."Passing up the punt, Hafley left it to the offense — and Willis pushed forward for 2 yards as the Dolphins celebrated."He trusted us," Willis said, "and we trusted him."Hafley, who grew up about 20 minutes north of MetLife Stadium in Montvale, got the win in front of about 30 friends and family members.The Jets, meanwhile, dropped to 0-8 against AFC East opponents under Aaron Glenn, including consecutive losses to New England and Miami."When it comes to this game, highly disappointed," Glenn said. "Disappointed in myself, first and foremost."Smith was 23 of 30 for 287 yards and three touchdowns, two to Taylor and another to Omar Cooper Jr., and an interception. Braelon Allen had 104 yards rushing.The Dolphins started quickly, marching 76 yards on seven plays and taking their first lead in any game this season on Willis' 7-yard touchdown pass to Douglas.It also ended New York's streak of not allowing any points on an opening possession in five straight games.But the Jets came right back with a 13-yard touchdown catch by Taylor — son of former Dolphins star and Pro Football Hall of Famer Jason Taylor — to tie it. It's the third straight game in which New York scored on its opening drive.Miami then went on a 14-play drive that was capped by a 1-yard touchdown run by Gordon, who finished with 103 yards rushing.New York was driving again on its next possession at the Miami 21 when Smith was intercepted by Michael Taaffe.The Dolphins' touchdown streak ended on their third possession when they went three-and-out. They got right back at it on their next drive, with Willis scoring on a 2-yard scramble with 6 seconds left in the first half.Allen gave New York some immediate second-half juice with a 27-yard run on the Jets' first play of the third quarter, but the drive stalled. Adding to the misery, Jason Sanders — a longtime Dolphins kicker in his first season with the Jets — hit the right upright on a 40-yard try.Cooper got New York's next drive started with a 60-yard reception, and ended it five plays later with a 3-yard touchdown catch to make it a one-score game at 21-14 with 5:50 left in the third quarter.The Jets later got to the Dolphins' 1, but couldn't punch it in on runs by Andrew Beck and Allen and settled for a 33-yard field goal when Smith was sacked on third down.Willis side-armed a short toss to Douglas, who tiptoed the sideline after the catch and raced for a 63-yard touchdown that put Miami up 28-17 with 4:44 remaining.Dolphins: RB Jaylen Wright left in the fourth quarter with an injured quadriceps. hurt his left shoulder in the third quarter. CB JuJu Brents left with a stinger in the second half, but returned in the fourth quarter.Jets: DT T'Vondre Sweat limped off with a knee injury late in the second quarter and didn't return.Dolphins: Host New England next Sunday.Jets: Host Las Vegas next Sunday.

The Miami Dolphins cornerback — known to friends and teammates as "Juju" — is in his fourth season in the NFL. Julius "Juju" Brents came to Miami in 2025, but his football journey began long before that.WPTV’s Eleanor Sheahan sat down with Brents this week in Miami Gardens to talk about his path to the pros, the mental demands of playing cornerback and how he's approaching the challenge of staying healthy. WATCH: Dolphins' Juju Brents talks injuries and ‘mental warfare’ of playing cornerback with WPTV's Eleanor Sheahan Off the top, Brents mentioned how the nickname “Juju” stuck."Funny thing about that, my mom gave me that nickname as a kid. So when I tell people my first name is Julius, they'd be like, are you for real? Like, because everybody calls me Juju. It's been like that since I was a child," Brents said.Brents said he has been playing football for a long time and he even remembers one of his first football drills."I got a vivid memory from when I was a kid. I remember they teach you how to tackle, right? They got like a, kind of like those little orange tall things, but it was red... Run up to that, they make you tackle and whatnot. I remember just running up to it and just kind of spear it. I'm supposed to be doing this, and it's like, I vividly remember that as a kid. So I still had that feeling when I come out here playing," Brents said.Now, roughly 20 years later, he's playing in the pros and thinking back to his 6-year-old self who is discovering the game for the first time."As a child, like I always told my mom, I think I want to be a football player and then it was like, no, I'm going to be a football player. Kind of build it to that," Brents said.On the field, Brents is a cornerback. When asked about the position and what being a defender entails, Brents said it's a constant mental battle."It's like mental warfare for sure. You know, being a corner is not an easy task at hand. Sometimes you lose a rep, but you don't have time to really sorrow in that loss. Your losses are on the grand scheme, like, you give up a big explosive play like that's noticeable, right? Compared to other positions. So I don't care who's in front of me. Being a competitor, I try to win every single snap," Brents said.Tackles are the forefront for defensive backs, but what is the secret to interceptions? Brents said it's all about preparation and watching film goes a long way."A lot of film study goes into it. Just intentionality for sure. You have to be big on the details and you got to be a little sad, you got to have some sadness to, you know, when those opportunities do come because it's not going to get a whole lot. But when they do come, you have to capitalize," Brents said.He said his in-game instincts are rooted in his work off the field. Brents credits his routine."Sure, you say naturally, and it can't be seen as natural, but at the end of the day, I like to say you just fall down to the level of your preparation," Brents said.Injuries have shaped much of his career, including his recent years in the NFL."I know early on in my career was tough. Going through college, I didn't have a whole lot of injuries. Then I get to the league and it was just like, injury after injury, trying to balance it, figure it out. So I faced a lot of adversity, but honestly, I think it was just a blessing in disguise. Now I feel like I got a better understanding of my body," Brents said.Throughout the conversation, Brents returned often to the mental side of the game — something he said he's had to grow into."I've had to grow in that space for sure. I'm not used to be one of the guys around thinking I'm so big and focusing on what everybody's saying and worried about it. Now I just let it be noise in the air, just having a clear focus, focusing on my path, my goals that I set out for myself, team goals, and just being focused on that," Brents said.For Brents, a fully healthy season would mean everything."I can't really control everything, so I'm trying to do my best to control my controllables. But I know the work that I have put in, and now that I do have the opportunity, like, I'm doing everything in my power to make sure I stay out here. It will mean everything to me just to finish this year strong, hopefully get some wins, which I know are coming here soon. Just being healthy," Brents said.Adding wins to the column and staying healthy are top of mind for Brents this season.

Ballet Palm Beach is bringing one of literature's most iconic stories to the stage this month with its original production of Mary Shelley's Frankenstein at the Kravis Center in West Palm Beach.The production runs Oct. Playhouse and reimagines Mary Shelley's classic novel through contemporary ballet. Ballet Palm Beach describes the performance as a dramatic exploration of ambition, abandonment and identity. The company is the professional ballet company of Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast.WATCH BELOW: Ballet Palm Beach brings 'Frankenstein' to the Kravis CenterAccording to Founding Artistic and Executive Director Colleen Smith, the story begins before Frankenstein's monster ever comes to life."It's a gorgeous production about Mary Shelley and her haunting book Frankenstein," Smith said.During the broadcast, Smith explained how the famous story was born during a gathering at Lake Geneva."They were gathered together on the shores of Lake Geneva on a stormy night, and Lord Byron was reading ghost stories and said, 'You know what, guys, let's create our own ghost stories,' and she did," Smith said. "First science fiction novel ever written by an 18-year-old woman."Dancer Leah Walker said audiences can expect something different from a traditional ballet."Most classical ballets are fantasy, but ours does follow the real story of Mary Shelley and her process as she writes it," Leah said. It's a very contemporary, very artistic take."The production is recommended for ages 9 and older and features two 45-minute acts separated by a 20-minute intermission.For audiences looking for a Halloween-season experience with a local arts connection, the performance offers a fresh take on a familiar tale. The production combines historical elements from Mary Shelley's life with the themes that have made Frankenstein one of the most enduring stories ever written.Tickets and performance information are available through Ballet Palm Beach and the Kravis Center. Blue Repose Foundation is launching a pilot program designed to help law enforcement officers and other public safety professionals recover from occupational stress through weekly float sessions, peer support and coping techniques.The startup nonprofit introduced the program at Float8 in Delray Beach, where Blue Repose Founder and President Bridget Coghlan discussed the pressures public safety professionals can encounter and the stigma that may prevent some from seeking support.“With our field, of course, we're exposed to traumas, long shift hours, and things of that nature,” Coghlan said. “We don't like to say mental health, so we just want to take care of the person and give them resources to do so within their professional life and their personal life at home.”Coghlan said the pilot will include five participants during its initial monthlong run at Transitions Wellness and Performance Center in Juno Beach.“They'll get a float session, one per week, followed by peer support and other coping decompression techniques to follow and hopefully it'll help them out,” Coghlan said.The program is part of Blue Repose Foundation’s developing mission to provide private, nonclinical restorative opportunities to law enforcement officers, corrections professionals and others working in public safety.Blue Repose says the foundation is being established in Martin County, with an initial focus on serving the Treasure Coast and Palm Beach County. Kristen Neves, the foundation’s director of community engagement and partnerships, said Blue Repose is seeking financial support to launch the pilot.“We're really looking for the community support right now to fund this program and get this pilot program up and going,” Neves said. “We just really want to get this out there and get those law enforcement supported.”Information about contributing to the program is available on the Blue Repose Foundation website.Float8 owner Matt Beck said the Delray Beach studio uses float cabins rather than pods.Float cabins contain shallow water with a high concentration of Epsom salt, allowing a person to remain buoyant. The private environment also reduces outside light, sound and other stimulation.“By reducing the effects of gravity and external stimulation on the body, it helps induce a meditative state, downregulate your nervous system, and help you recover from those stressful situations that our law enforcement officers face so often,” Beck said.Blue Repose describes the float experience as one component of a broader program that will include peer support and additional coping and decompression techniques.Public safety professionals can encounter trauma, long shifts, and sustained stress while serving their communities. Blue Repose’s pilot reflects an effort to give participants structured time to decompress while connecting them with support beyond the float cabin.The initial program will allow Blue Repose to begin evaluating its approach with a small group of participants as the nonprofit works to secure community funding.The foundation’s broader goal is to help professionals take care of themselves in both their working and personal lives while making recovery a more accepted part of public service.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI.
