Three seniors at Alexander W. Dreyfoos School of the Arts have created Prodigy Pro, a free artificial intelligence platform designed to help students turn their ideas into real-world ventures.Co-founders Aiden Azoy and Anthony Tan and Head of Design Mia Rubio developed the platform after attending South Florida business networking events and realizing how few students were in the room.WATCH: Dreyfoos seniors build free AI platform for student entrepreneurs“We attended networking events and we noticed, why are we the youngest people in the room?” Azoy said. “There are so many talented students in our communities where they’re able to pursue their professional careers outside of school.”The students said they wanted to give young people a way to explore their interests, develop practical ideas and participate in West Palm Beach’s growing business community.The founders attend Dreyfoos in downtown West Palm Beach, where new development and the arrival of major companies have fueled the area’s growing reputation as “Wall Street South.”“We go to Dreyfoos, and literally hundreds of feet away are these huge constructions of Related Ross, companies like ServiceNow or even Citadel moving down to South Florida,” Tan said. “We’re right at the forefront of this new business center that is becoming West Palm Beach.”Tan said the students attempted to connect with professionals at local gatherings but struggled to find opportunities intended for people their age.“We tried to go to these meetings, and a lot of the time there wouldn’t be any opportunity for us,” Tan said. “So that’s why we wanted to create our own.”Prodigy Pro was built to help students take the first steps toward developing projects and businesses.“Prodigy Pro is a free AI entrepreneurship platform that helps a student take their idea from an idea to the final product,” Tan said.Azoy said the team created the platform after noticing that many students were not taking their ideas beyond the classroom.“Prodigy Pro is a way for students to build real ventures outside of school and be able to pursue their professional interests,” Azoy said. “We noticed that not enough students are getting out there and really putting their ideas out into the world. We gave them the ability to do that.”Users enter information about an idea and the problem they hope to solve. The platform’s AI then helps organize the concept and identify potential next steps.Rubio designed the user interface and worked to make the process understandable for students who may have little or no previous business experience.“You upload your information and the idea that you really want to pursue,” Rubio said. “And the AI will help you guide and shape and really tell you what your next step is, as well as create roadmaps, reminders and just really help your venture get off the ground.”The platform divides the development process into smaller sections and tasks.“With Prodigy [Pro], we wanted to make the next step super easy and attainable,” Rubio said. “So we grouped things into different sections and made each task super easy for the user to understand, so they know what to do next with their venture.”During a demonstration, the students used concerns about a school bus route to show how a user could enter a problem and explore possible efficiencies. “You input your information, and it really gives you the next steps, what you should do, and you can ask the AI to help develop your venture,” Rubio said.The founders said making Prodigy Pro free was central to their mission. Azoy said students should have access to the same entrepreneurial tools regardless of their school or community’s resources.“It’s completely free for students, and we want to stress that because we want to basically give the message that a student in an underprivileged school or community should have the same exact resources as, you know, a student in a resourced school,” Azoy said.According to the students, Prodigy Pro has grown to more than 15,000 users in 20 countries.The team also competed in the Mott Million Dollar Challenge, a national student entrepreneurship competition.“A few months ago in May, we competed in the Mott Million Dollar Challenge, where we won $7,500 for our venture,” Tan said.Tan said the prize money was reinvested into Prodigy Pro.“A lot of it went into the development of the platform, going through the UI, the back end, also enabling the AI to be free for other students,” he said.The three founders are seniors preparing for life after high school, but they said Prodigy Pro will continue.Asked whether the platform would remain after graduation, Rubio responded, “Yes, of course. It’ll remain to be a free platform for our users.”For Azoy, the larger goal is to show young people that they do not have to wait to begin developing their professional interests.“We really think that it’s important for them to be showing up and, you know, building ventures that really matter because every student has creativity in an underprivileged or privileged school,” Azoy said.The students’ work comes as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into education, business and everyday problem-solving. By making the platform free, the Dreyfoos seniors hope more young people will be able to turn their creativity into action and create opportunities of their own.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. After noticing worsening water quality while rowing, South Fork High School senior Bianca Bernhard founded the Martin Oyster Restoration Initiative (MORI) a student-led nonprofit that recycles oyster shells to support restoration projects in local waterways.“The water quality got really bad,” Bernhard told WPTV’s T.A. “That’s due to discharges from Lake Okeechobee, so I decided to do something with the extra free time.”The initiative, known as MORI, collects oyster shells from local restaurants. Volunteers at South Fork High School then help dry and cure the shells so they can be used in restoration projects.WATCH: Stuart student leads oyster restoration mission“I recycle a lot of shells from local restaurants,” Bernhard said. “These local shells will help create new reef structures like what I’m holding right here, and those reef structures will grow new oysters which will filter the water.”South Fork High School students and teachers have joined Bernhard’s conservation effort through the school’s marine science, construction and agriculture programs.During the WPTV segment, Jennifer Inostroza, a teacher at South Fork High School, explained that the school helps cure and dry the oyster shells so they are ready for future projects.Information provided by the Martin County School District says MORI has recruited more than 60 students and teachers and amassed approximately 1,600 pounds of oyster shell.The district says participating students can earn honor credits through South Fork High School’s Marine Sciences program.The recycled shells do not immediately return to the water. They must first be transported, dried and cured before they can be incorporated into approved restoration structures.According to Bernhard, those structures provide places where new oysters can grow. She said the oysters then help filter and clean the surrounding water.MORI is also collaborating with Docks for a Clean Lagoon, a nonprofit that installs vertical oyster gardens. According to Bernhard’s Go Blue Awards narrative, shells cured by South Fork volunteers have been used in the creation of vertical oyster gardens intended for the Indian River Lagoon.Bernhard is a finalist in the Blue Hatchling Youth category of Loggerhead Marinelife Center’s 2026 Go Blue Awards.“Bianca is one of our finalists for the Go Blue Hatchling Awards,” said Audrey Padgett, VP of Marketing, at Loggerhead Marinelife Center, told WPTV. “We’ve had nominees from all over the world. So it’s really amazing to see someone selected by this independent panel of judges here in our backyard for the work that she’s doing to improve ocean conservation and ecosystems right here.”The annual awards recognize young people, individuals, businesses and nonprofit organizations making contributions to ocean conservation.The 2026 Go Blue Awards ceremony is scheduled for 11:30 a.m. 30, at the Kravis Center for the Performing Arts in West Palm Beach.Bernhard’s work comes as MORI prepares for its next phase. According to her Go Blue Awards narrative, she aims to expand the initiative to three additional local schools during the 2026-27 school year.She also plans to pursue oyster restoration research with the Florida Oceanographic Society and work with students to develop additional structures for restoration projects.For Bernhard, the project began with something she saw while rowing. It has since grown into a broader effort that gives students a hands-on role in responding to the environmental challenges facing their community.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A 15-year-old was arrested and faces 11 counts of attempted second-degree murder and possession of a firearm by a delinquent in connection with a mass shooting Saturday night that left 11 people wounded, Tallahassee Police Chief Lawrence Revell said Monday morning.The investigation suggests a physical altercation took place among “individuals known to one another” before shots were fired near the Florida A&M football stadium, Revell said.“At this stage of the investigation, none of the victims appear to have been the intended targets,” the police chief said.The investigation remains active and additional arrests are possible, Revell said.Six juveniles, including an 11-year-old, are among the injured, Revell said late Saturday. No deaths have been reported.RELATED STORY | 11-year-old, other minors among 11 shot near Florida A&M University stadiumThe off-campus shooting took place hours after a homecoming football game at Bragg Memorial Stadium, where the Golden Lions of the University of Arkansas-Pine Bluff beat the Florida A&M Rattlers 31-28. It’s unclear whether the shooting was connected to the game.In addition to those shot, a victim’s grandmother was injured while fleeing.As of Sunday morning, five people had been released from the hospital, while six remained hospitalized, Tallahassee police said. Of those still being treated, one was in critical condition, police said.There have been at least 383 mass shootings in the US so far this year, according to the Gun Violence Archive, which, like CNN, defines a mass shooting as one in which four or more people are shot, not including the shooter.Homecoming events at Florida A&M, a historically Black university with nearly 10,000 students, took place throughout the past week and were scheduled to conclude Sunday, according to the university’s homecoming schedule.Saturday night’s shooting on Perry Street likely stemmed from a fight between two to three people, the police chief said, and the department’s Violent Crimes Unit will lead the investigation.Tallahassee police detectives have reviewed digital evidence and canvassed the area, police said in a statement Sunday.“We need our community’s help. No detail is too small, and no piece of information should go unreported,” the statement said. “If you know something, please share it with our detectives. Your information could be the key to holding those responsible accountable.”Investigators established a tip hotline and a link for people to submit evidence.“As our detectives work to determine exactly what happened and identify those responsible, we remain committed to getting answers for these families.”Florida A&M President Marva Johnson encouraged anyone with information to call the tip line, saying the Tallahassee police are leading the investigation.“To our Rattler family and our surrounding Tallahassee community, I share your outrage and profound sadness at the senseless and despicable shooting that took place near our FAMU campus last night,” Johnson said in a statement Sunday evening.“To all the victims, please know that we are with you and we are praying for your recovery in body, mind and spirit,” she said. “We have reached out to the members of our FAMU family who were injured in this tragic incident to offer our care and support.”Tallahassee Mayor John Dailey called the incident a “truly horrific and heartbreaking tragedy.”“Tonight and in the days ahead, the FAMU family is not alone. Our entire community stands with you,” Dailey wrote on X.Stephanie Walters, who was selling HBCU apparel during homecoming, said she also heard shots.“People are just scared,” she told CNN affiliate WCTV. “If you were out here, you heard the gunshots. There was no doubt in my mind that somebody was injured.”Raymond Isham said he had just left campus when the shooting happened, and he was concerned about his daughter, who was in the area where the shooting occurred.“She’s obviously going to have to process through this,” Isham told WCTV, “and we’re going to be there with her to walk through this.”The-CNN-Wire™ & © 2026 Cable News Network, Inc., a Warner Bros.

King tides flooded streets and reached homes across Palm Beach County on Monday, while beach and road closures were reported as more high tides were expected through Wednesday. In Palm City, flooding made SW Dyer Point Road impassable. Martin County Sheriff’s Office deputies brought in three high-water vehicles to help reach anyone stranded in a vehicle or home. Flooding also was reported on SW 34th Street and Cornell Avenue. One driver told CBS12 the water was about waist-deep in part of the area. Resident Terresa Baldwin said water came up around both the front and back of her home, and that Monday’s flooding was the worst she had seen in eight years. Baldwin also raised concerns about the water’s source and smell. This is not only runoff water, it’s sewage and it’s bad and you can smell it, she said. Deputies urged people to avoid flooded areas and not to drive through standing water. These vehicles can travel through several feet of water safely, Martin County Sheriff’s Office Lt. Flooding also reached Flagler Drive in downtown West Palm Beach and Sunset Avenue on Palm Beach Island, where water covered parts of the roadway and disrupted pedestrians and cyclists. In Boynton Beach, flooding led to road closures, including at Ocean Avenue and Federal Highway. The Ocean Inlet Marina also closed because of high tides. In Boca Raton, water reached a Cub Scout pack’s campsite at Spanish River Park, prompting campers to move supplies to higher ground. Elsewhere, Midtown Beach was temporarily closed because of large surf and high tides. The northbound lane of South Ocean Boulevard between Chilean and Australian avenues was scheduled to close from 10 a.m. to noon while crews moved a lifeguard tower. Delray Beach officials raised red flags because of high surf and flooding, and the Juno Beach Pier remained closed because of damage from a recent offshore surge and high surf. See also: 15-year-old FAMU shooting suspect ordered to be held as prosecutors seek adult charges A coastal flood warning covers low-lying areas near the water in Palm Beach, Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties. The National Weather Service said the warning runs through 8 p.m. Wednesday in coastal Palm Beach County and 2 a.m. Thursday in coastal Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties. The forecast high tides were: Monday: 9:06 p.m. The sheriff’s office advised residents not to drive through floodwater and to call 911 if they need emergency assistance.

A young man from the Midwest with South Florida roots describes how Andrew Burnette moved from Michigan around the age of 12 and found home on the football field in Martin County. "I played football my whole life, and I can say football is a little harder in Florida than it is in Michigan," said Burnette. WATCH BELOW: Local football standout gets one more shot at college football While football was his first sport, during his high school days at Jensen Beach High School, he fell in love with takedowns and pins. "I wasn't zoned for that school, but I went there for wrestling originally; that was my first passion," said Burnette. While he was doing well in wrestling, football kept calling to him. "Moving through high school, I knew football was what I wanted to do," said Burnette. He established himself as a force at Jensen Beach High School, but he didn't receive much interest from college football programs, similar to many Treasure Coast football recruits. "One of my main struggles was recruitment out of high school, because I felt like our area was a little under-recruited," said Burnette. Betting on himself, he decided to play at Highland Community College in Kansas. Burnette played in nine games and rushed for 340 yards and two touchdowns, but he still wasn't on any other college football program's radar. "I transferred to Independence Junior College, and I was cut from the team," said Burnette. Independence was featured on the hit Netflix show Last Chance U, but once his chance there was short-lived, he reached out to Keiser University in West Palm Beach. "I spoke with the coach there and told him, 'You guys offered me in high school,' and he said, 'I don't really remember. Send me your film.' He saw my film and said, 'Hey, bring it,'" said Burnette. And he did "bring it." In the two years he played at Keiser, he rushed for over 2,300 yards and 30 touchdowns. With stats like that, Division I programs finally came calling, starting with Louisiana Tech. "Last year I played there; it was my first year at the Division I level, and then my eligibility ran out," said Burnette. At the time, the NCAA granted student-athletes only four years of eligibility unless they were injured, so Burnette rolled up his sleeves and got to work. "I called my dad and told him, 'Hey, I need to do something. I can't just sit here,' so I went and worked with my dad in Michigan," said Burnette. He worked with his dad at a steel mill in Detroit for a few months, but this summer the NCAA announced the 5-in-5 rule, meaning student-athletes can compete for up to five seasons across a continuous five-year period. So he hired a lawyer and went to court with the NCAA to get his final year of eligibility, and they granted him one last year, and now he's making the most of it. "It was amazing; I would rather play football than do anything, and for me to have this opportunity again, it's a blessing," said Burnette.

Lucie County Fire District firefighter who died unexpectedly Saturday morning has been identified as Austin Hodge, a firefighter paramedic and nine-year veteran of the department.The fire district announced Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk during a shift change. He was taken to the hospital and passed away.WATCH REPORT BELOW: St. Lucie County firefighter dies on duty"Today, our St. Lucie County Fire District family mourns the loss of one of our own," the district said in a statement. In the hours following his death, firefighters, the department's Honor Guard and fellow first responders gathered to honor Hodge and support one another. The district said the response reflected the strong bond shared throughout the fire service. The district thanked the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Fort Pierce Police Department, Port St. Lucie Police Department and peer support teams from Martin and Indian River counties for providing assistance and standing alongside firefighters during the difficult day."Together, they offered strength, compassion, and support while ensuring Austin was honored with the dignity and respect he deserves," the district said. The district said its thoughts are with Hodge's family, loved ones and everyone who served alongside him. They respectfully ask that Hodge's family be given privacy during this time."We are deeply grateful to our fellow first responders and community for the outpouring of support during this tremendous loss," the district said. "Today and always, we stand together." The tragedy comes more than a year after the community mourned the sudden loss of his brother, Jarius Hodge, 26, who was also a St. Lucie County firefighter and died from septic shock in July 2025.The district said it will share information on funeral and memorial services in coordination with the family when it becomes available.

Family and friends are mourning St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge, a man those closest to him describe as endlessly positive and devoted to serving his community. A funeral procession for Hodge left the Medical Examiner’s Office in Fort Pierce at 2 p.m. Monday and traveled to Stone Brothers Funeral Home. Lucie County Sheriff's Office went to the station at 7:25 a.m. 24, regarding a "full cardiac arrest," and Hoge was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. His death comes about 15 months after his younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County Fire District firefighter and paramedic, died in July 2025 after falling ill during a shift. The district honored Jarius with line-of-duty honors. After his brother’s death, Austin spent months searching for answers. He told CBS12 News in January that Jarius caught the flu from a patient and died hours after arriving at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie, struggling to breathe. Austin said medical records showed doctors made critical mistakes, including needing three attempts to intubate his brother. CBS12 reached out to the hospital at the time and did not receive a response before that story was published. Because Jarius was over 25 and had no spouse or children, Florida’s so-called free kill law barred his family from suing for medical malpractice. Austin pushed state lawmakers to repeal it and started a petition in his brother’s honor. He said the fight was about accountability, not money. Bernard Taylor has known Austin since their school days in Sebastian. Taylor was a senior and Austin a freshman when they met at the Boys and Girls Club, where Taylor worked as a counselor and Austin was one of the kids he mentored. Taylor said Austin always wanted to keep up with the older kids, and the two formed a bond that lasted for years. Later, when Taylor decided to change careers, Austin was one of the first people he called. Taylor said Austin supported him through becoming a firefighter, from answering questions to helping him with his conditioning. Just a ball of positive energy. A smile that lights up the room. No matter what you’re going through, he had the right words to kind of get you through it, Taylor said. Taylor said he spoke with Austin about a week before his death to make sure he was doing well. He said he is most heartbroken for Austin’s mother, who has now lost both of her sons. That’s one of the strongest people I’ve ever met in my life. I don’t know if I can hold it together if I was her, Taylor said. Bonnie Hill, a family friend who helped raise Austin’s mother, said she has been by her side and that the family is leaning on its faith and a strong circle of support. I say on my watch, I’m not going to let you die. You’re going to live, and we’re going to get through this, Hill said of what she has told Austin’s mother. Hill said that faith is what is carrying the family now. See also: King tides cause coastal flooding, beach closures in Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast We believe God even in this. We believe God, and we stand on the promises because they won’t fail, Hill said. Taylor said he hopes people remember Austin for his love of serving others. He was a person who loved what he did. He was a person who loved serving his community, Taylor said. Lucie County Fire District has not released details about Austin Hodge’s death.

After months of controversy, the St. Lucie County Fire District Board voted Wednesday to fire longtime Chief Jeff Lee, following an emotional meeting filled with calls for change and coming less than two weeks after the firefighters' union released the results of a no-confidence vote in the district's top leaders. The meeting was packed with firefighters, union members, retirees and residents, many urged the board to change the district's leadership. Among them was Taylor Baldwin, who pointed to the dozens of supporters wearing yellow shirts throughout the room. Look at everyone wearing yellow," Baldwin told commissioners. "These are not people who want to see the fire district fail. These are people who love this department enough to stand up and beg you to save it." The decision marks the latest development in a controversy that began this summer after a hazing investigation led to the firing of three veteran firefighters and the suspension of two others . The district determined the conduct amounted to hazing, while the firefighters and their union have argued it was consensual horseplay. A Fort Pierce Police Department investigation found no criminal violations. The union is pursuing arbitration to get the three firefighters reinstated . The issue later escalated into a no-confidence vote organized by IAFF Local 1377. According to the union, 423 of its 517 dues-paying members participated. Lee received 314 no-confidence votes and 108 confidence votes, with 74.23% of participants voting they no longer had confidence in his leadership. Several speakers criticized both district leadership and the board's handling of the controversy. "You participated in this cover-up. You protected the lies and you profoundly failed the people you are elected to serve," another resident Katie told the board. Lee, who joined the department in 1997 after serving in the U.S. Navy and became the district's 14th fire chief in May 2023, was not present for Wednesday's meeting. Commissioners spent more than 30 minutes debating whether Lee should be fired with or without cause. Ultimately, the board voted to terminate him without cause, triggering the severance provisions in his contract. "I think we still have to come to the determination of what exactly the final total is of the severance," board member James Clasby said after the vote. "We will only pay what we are legally required to." Those who supported Lee's removal said the district needs a fresh start. "I feel like a weight is lifted," Commissioner Jamie Fowler said. "Firing someone is never an easy decision, regardless of all the factors that come into play. So I feel like we've sort of taken a step in the right direction." Following Lee's termination, the board voted 4-3 to appoint Deputy Chief Paul Langel as interim chief while a search for a permanent replacement begins. The board is also moving forward with hiring outside legal counsel and discussing the process for selecting the district's next chief. See also: Former PBSO dispatcher sentenced after 2023 head-on DUI crash that killed mother This is not the first time the board has faced this choice. In 2017, after a union no-confidence vote, the board accepted then Chief Buddy Emerson’s retirement effective immediately and paid him severance through the end of his contract.

hero.headline: Palm City flooding could worsen with Monday night high tide, sheriff’s office warns
hero.body:
Strong winds and king tides flooded parts of Palm City off Dyer Point Road on Monday, and the Martin County sheriff’s office warned that high tide later Monday night could worsen conditions. Parts of the area were completely underwater before the water retreated.

Lt. Dave Rosko said the sheriff’s office has three high-water vehicles ready for rescue efforts and urged residents not to drive through floodwater. “Understand the limitations of your vehicle and do not drive through the high waters,” Rosko said. “If your vehicle gets disabled there, it may turn into a rescue event where we need to come out and ensure your safety.” He also urged residents of coastal communities to be aware of future tides before traveling.

Terresa Baldwin, who lives off Dyer Point Road, said the area had been flooded for a few hours before the water receded. She also had flooding in her backyard along one of the finger canals, with water over her dock and into her new patio. “You could smell the sewage; it was really stinky, it was bad,” Baldwin said. She also reported seeing dead copperheads in the floodwater.

Baldwin remained concerned about more flooding over the next few days despite the retreating water. “The biggest concern for us is getting water from both sides. What do you do, especially when you're trying to sleep, and you don't know if the water's going to come up more or what's going to get damaged at night when you really can't see,” Baldwin said.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce procession honors St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge
hero.teaser: Monday’s funeral procession traveled from the Medical Examiner’s Office to Stone Brothers Funeral Home. Loved ones remembered Hodge for his positive outlook and devotion to serving his community.
hero.body:
A funeral procession for St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge, who died while on duty Oct. 24, left the Medical Examiner’s Office in Fort Pierce at 2 p.m. Monday and traveled to Stone Brothers Funeral Home. Family and friends remembered him as a source of encouragement who loved serving his community and helped others pursue careers in firefighting.

Bernard Taylor knew Hodge since their school days in Sebastian. Taylor was a senior working as a counselor at the Boys and Girls Club when he met Hodge, a freshman he mentored. Hodge always wanted to keep up with the older kids, Taylor said, and their bond lasted for years. When Taylor later decided to change careers, Hodge was one of the first people he called. Hodge answered questions and helped Taylor with conditioning as he worked toward becoming a firefighter. “Just a ball of positive energy. A smile that lights up the room. No matter what you’re going through, he had the right words to kind of get you through it,” Taylor said.

Taylor said he spoke with Hodge about a week before his death to make sure he was doing well. He said he was most heartbroken for Hodge’s mother, who has now lost both of her sons. Bonnie Hill, a family friend who helped raise Hodge’s mother, said she has been by her side. Hill said the family is relying on faith and a strong circle of support.

Hodge’s younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County Fire District firefighter and paramedic, died in July 2025 after falling ill during a shift. The district honored Jarius with line-of-duty honors. Austin spent months searching for answers after his brother’s death and pushed state lawmakers to repeal Florida’s so-called free kill law. Because Jarius was over 25 and had no spouse or children, the law barred his family from suing for medical malpractice. Austin started a petition in his brother’s honor and said his fight was about accountability, not money. Taylor said he hopes people remember Austin’s commitment to others: “He was a person who loved what he did. He was a person who loved serving his community.”
hero.article_text: Family and friends are mourning St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge, a man those closest to him describe as endlessly positive and devoted to serving his community. A funeral procession for Hodge left the Medical Examiner’s Office in Fort Pierce at 2 p.m. Monday and traveled to Stone Brothers Funeral Home. Lucie County Sheriff's Office went to the station at 7:25 a.m. 24, regarding a "full cardiac arrest," and Hoge was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. His death comes about 15 months after his younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County Fire District firefighter and paramedic, died in July 2025 after falling ill during a shift. The district honored Jarius with line-of-duty honors. After his brother’s death, Austin spent months searching for answers. He told CBS12 News in January that Jarius caught the flu from a patient and died hours after arriving at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie, struggling to breathe. Austin said medical records showed doctors made critical mistakes, including needing three attempts to intubate his brother. CBS12 reached out to the hospital at the time and did not receive a response before that story was published. Because Jarius was over 25 and had no spouse or children, Florida’s so-called free kill law barred his family from suing for medical malpractice. Austin pushed state lawmakers to repeal it and started a petition in his brother’s honor. He said the fight was about accountability, not money. Bernard Taylor has known Austin since their school days in Sebastian. Taylor was a senior and Austin a freshman when they met at the Boys and Girls Club, where Taylor worked as a counselor and Austin was one of the kids he mentored. Taylor said Austin always wanted to keep up with the older kids, and the two formed a bond that lasted for years. Later, when Taylor decided to change careers, Austin was one of the first people he called. Taylor said Austin supported him through becoming a firefighter, from answering questions to helping him with his conditioning. Just a ball of positive energy. A smile that lights up the room. No matter what you’re going through, he had the right words to kind of get you through it, Taylor said. Taylor said he spoke with Austin about a week before his death to make sure he was doing well. He said he is most heartbroken for Austin’s mother, who has now lost both of her sons. That’s one of the strongest people I’ve ever met in my life. I don’t know if I can hold it together if I was her, Taylor said. Bonnie Hill, a family friend who helped raise Austin’s mother, said she has been by her side and that the family is leaning on its faith and a strong circle of support. I say on my watch, I’m not going to let you die. You’re going to live, and we’re going to get through this, Hill said of what she has told Austin’s mother. Hill said that faith is what is carrying the family now. See also: King tides cause coastal flooding, beach closures in Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast We believe God even in this. We believe God, and we stand on the promises because they won’t fail, Hill said. Taylor said he hopes people remember Austin for his love of serving others. He was a person who loved what he did. He was a person who loved serving his community, Taylor said. Lucie County Fire District has not released details about Austin Hodge’s death.

hero.headline: Flooding blocks SW Dyer Point Road in Palm City; deputies deploy high-water vehicles
hero.body:
King tide flooding made SW Dyer Point Road in Palm City impassable Monday, prompting Martin County Sheriff’s Office deputies to bring in three high-water vehicles to help reach people stranded in vehicles or homes. The flooding came as a coastal flood warning remained in effect for coastal Martin County through 2 a.m. Thursday.

Flooding also was reported on SW 34th Street and Cornell Avenue. One driver described water about waist-deep in part of the area. Resident Terresa Baldwin said water surrounded the front and back of her home and described Monday’s flooding as the worst she had seen in eight years. Baldwin also raised concerns about the water’s smell and said she believed it contained sewage rather than only runoff.

The National Weather Service’s coastal flood warning covers low-lying areas near the water in Palm Beach, Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties. The warning runs through 2 a.m. Thursday in coastal Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties and through 8 p.m. Wednesday in coastal Palm Beach County. More high tides were expected through Wednesday, with Monday’s high tide forecast for 9:06 p.m.

Deputies urged people to avoid flooded areas and not to drive through standing water. The sheriff’s office advised residents to call 911 if they need emergency assistance.

In Palm City, flooding made SW Dyer Point Road impassable. Martin County Sheriff’s Office deputies brought in three high-water vehicles to help reach anyone stranded in a vehicle or home. hero.headline: Man arrested on loitering, prowling and trespassing charges in Hobe Sound
hero.teaser: Joseph Oswald, 28, was arrested after residents on Crooked Oak Avenue called 911 about suspicious activity, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office.
hero.body:
Joseph Oswald, 28, was arrested on charges of loitering, prowling and trespassing after residents reported a disturbance in a Hobe Sound neighborhood, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office.

Residents along the 6000 block of Crooked Oak Avenue called 911 after Oswald was yelling at people and wandering through the neighborhood, deputies said. Responding deputies found Oswald, who appeared to be under the influence of an unknown substance, according to the sheriff's office.

The sheriff's office said Oswald had been released from prison 11 days before his arrest and had as many as 14 prior arrests in Martin County, on charges ranging from grand theft and burglary to loitering and prowling. The agency praised residents for quickly reporting the activity, saying community reports of suspicious behavior help keep neighborhoods safe.

hero.headline: Coastal flood warning covers St. Lucie County through 2 a.m. Thursday
hero.body:
A coastal flood warning remains in effect for coastal St. Lucie County until 2 a.m. Thursday as king tides are expected to produce the season’s highest tides along Florida’s Atlantic coast. Low-lying locations close to the water are at risk of flooding, particularly where drainage is poor and around high tide. According to the National Weather Service, coastal Martin and Indian River counties are also under the warning until 2 a.m. Thursday. The warning for coastal Palm Beach County lasts until 8 p.m. Wednesday. Monday’s highest tide is expected at 9:06 p.m.

In Palm City, flooding has made SW Dyer Point Road impassable, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office reported. Flooding was also reported on SW 34th Street and Cornell Avenue. Images released by the Sheriff’s Office show widespread water across streets, with people walking through water reaching their ankles. The agency is sending high-water rescue vehicles to assist people stranded in homes or vehicles. Residents should stay away from the flooded area and call 911 if they need emergency help. Drivers should never attempt to cross a flooded road and should turn around instead. A separate video shows flooding on Indian River Drive, with a car traveling through the water.

In Boynton Beach, heavy flooding has closed the intersection of Ocean Avenue and Federal Highway. Drivers are being asked to stay clear of the intersection and take other routes. Officials plan to provide an update after the water drops and the intersection reopens. High tides have also forced the closure of Ocean Inlet Marina. Midtown Beach is temporarily closed because large surf and unusually high tides have made beach access unsafe, officials said. On South Ocean Boulevard, the northbound lane between Chilean Avenue and Australian Avenue will close from 10 a.m. to noon so crews can move a lifeguard tower.

Other coastal recreation areas are also affected. Delray Beach officials say red flags are flying at the city’s beach because of high surf and flooding. The Juno Beach Pier is closed until further notice after sustaining damage from a recent offshore surge and high surf. Those closures accompany the coastal flood warnings covering Palm Beach, Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties. With flooding more likely near high tide, residents in low-lying waterfront areas and places with poor drainage should avoid flooded roads. The safety message for motorists is to turn back rather than drive into floodwater.

cards.headline: Buc-ee's gets site plan approval in St. Lucie County; building permits under review
cards.teaser: The proposed 120-pump travel center off Indrio Road and Interstate 95 still has county staff comments to address. Buc-ee's website lists a 2027 opening.
cards.body:
The proposed 120-pump Buc-ee's travel center off Indrio Road and Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County has received site plan approval, and its building permits are under review, county Planning Director Ben Balser said last week.

Responding to questions from a St. Lucie County commissioner, Balser said the county is ready to move forward once Buc-ee's addresses the remaining comments from county staff. Buc-ee's website continues to list the location as opening in 2027.

Plans for the travel center were first announced in 2023. The Texas-based chain is known for its large stores and expansive fueling areas. The St. Lucie County location would bring Buc-ee's to the Treasure Coast.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge dies while on duty Oct. 24
hero.teaser: Austin Hodge served at Station 9 and had been with the district for more than nine years. The district will share memorial arrangements as they are finalized.
hero.body:
St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge died while on duty Saturday, Oct. 24, the St. Lucie County Fire District announced, calling his death a profound loss to the department and the fire service community. Hodge was assigned to Station 9 and had served the community for more than nine years after joining the district on July 17, 2017. Neighboring Indian River County Fire Rescue also shared condolences following his unexpected death Saturday morning. The circumstances surrounding his death have not been released.

Hodge’s death came more than a year after his younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic, died on July 22, 2025, at age 26. The brothers shared a close bond and a passion for serving their community. Austin had described Jarius as his best friend and said they enjoyed working alongside each other. He described his younger brother as someone who loved his family, his community and his country, loved going to work and pushed Austin to keep going.

Austin had said Jarius became ill after catching the flu from a patient at work in July 2025. According to Austin’s account, Jarius went to Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie on July 22 because he was struggling to breathe and died hours later. Austin said his brother had been healthy before becoming ill. He alleged that medical staff made critical errors while treating Jarius, including taking three attempts to intubate him. Those claims were allegations Austin raised while seeking accountability for his brother’s death.

Austin also spoke publicly about Florida’s medical malpractice laws, arguing that restrictions on who can pursue certain wrongful-death claims prevented his family from seeking legal accountability. He emphasized that the family wanted the physicians held accountable rather than financial compensation. Following Austin’s death, the St. Lucie County Fire District asked the public to respect his family as they grieve. The district said information about memorial arrangements would be shared as details are finalized. It also said additional information about ways to honor his service would be shared in coordination with his family.

hero.headline: Donalds, Jolly outline differences on taxes, schools and data centers in Florida race
hero.body:
Republican Byron Donalds and Democrat David Jolly outlined different approaches to property-tax revenue, school accountability and data centers in closing interviews as they campaigned across Florida. A University of North Florida poll released last week found the governor’s race statistically tied. Donalds, a Republican congressman, wants to build on the policies of outgoing Gov. Ron DeSantis, while Jolly, who served in Congress as a Republican during the 2010s, is emphasizing housing, health care and education.

Donalds supports continuing Florida’s Department of Government Efficiency, which DeSantis created by executive order in 2025 and which has audited multiple counties. He said that work would be important if voters approve Amendment 3, which would raise homestead tax exemptions and reduce local revenue. Donalds said he has committed to a funding formula to help fiscally constrained counties whose budgets would change significantly. Jolly personally opposes the amendment but said he would support voters’ decision if it passes. “I think we all want the math behind Amendment 3 to work, but it just doesn't,” Jolly said.

Both candidates support keeping universal school vouchers. Jolly also wants greater transparency requirements for charter schools and higher pay for public school teachers. He said schools accepting vouchers should provide the same services, meet the same standards and face the same measures as public schools. Asked whether charter school financial records should be public, Donalds emphasized student achievement, including attainment in math and reading, along with ACT and SAT scores. “I think that's the accountability and the transparency that parents are looking for in the state of Florida, because at the end of the day, they're looking to make sure that the output is where it needs to be.”

The candidates also differ on data center construction. Jolly supports a moratorium, while Donalds said local governments should decide whether to allow the facilities. Donalds said that when local governments approve data centers, the state should protect water resources and ensure utility costs are not passed to consumers. Jolly said he wants to work across party lines on his broader agenda, arguing that expanding health care access would reduce costs and that investments in public education and stable housing would strengthen the economy. Donalds also pledged to continue immigration enforcement and expand government-efficiency reviews to local governments and state agencies throughout Florida.
hero.article_text: The race to be Florida's next governor is a competitive one — a statistical tie, according to a poll released last week by the University of North Florida.I caught up with Republican Byron Donalds and Democrat David Jolly as they each campaigned across the state, pitching different visions of Florida's future to voters.Donalds, a Republican congressman, told me in a video call from his campaign bus on the road that he wants to build on the policies he likes from Gov. Ron DeSantis' outgoing administration."We live in a great state, and what has separated us from the other states is we continue to choose common sense conservative policy," Donalds said.That includes immigration enforcement."We're going to continue that mission here in the great state of Florida because we are going to continue to follow the law. I think that's the appropriate use of state authority and state powers," Donalds said.It also includes Florida's Department of Government Efficiency, which DeSantis formed through an executive order in 2025 and has since conducted audits of multiple counties across Florida."We are going to DOGE all governments, both local and state agencies in the state of Florida, because it's not our tax money. It belongs to the people of Florida. We need to make sure that government lives within its means, the way families have to live within their means," Donalds said.Donalds told me that effort will be important if Amendment 3 passes, raising homestead tax exemptions and reducing local revenue. I asked him whether, as governor, he would be prepared if some of the municipalities that need help come to Tallahassee asking for it."Yes, we will, and we've already made a public commitment to the fiscally constrained counties in the state of Florida," Donalds said. "Those that we know that their budgets are going to change in a major way, that we're prepared to provide a funding formula for those fiscally constrained counties so that they can be able to make ends meet."Jolly, a Democrat who served as a Republican in Congress during the 2010s, visited WPTV as his campaign traveled through Palm Beach County. He has said he personally opposes Amendment 3, but will support the will of the voters if it passes."I think we all want the math behind Amendment 3 to work, but it just doesn't," Jolly said.Florida hasn't elected a Democrat as governor since the 1990s. I asked Jolly why he thinks that is and why he believes his campaign could overcome that."Look, we're a state that trended Republican, particularly in the last eight years, and we know by voter registration it's still a predominantly Republican state," Jolly said. "I think we're in a moment most akin to a 1974 post-Watergate moment, where voters are saying, 'Burn the ships. Let's go in a new direction.'"Jolly said that direction should be simple."Housing, healthcare, education, and no data centers. "The answers are not in ideology. The answers are in solutions."He also said he wants to reach across the aisle to achieve those goals."If we expand health care access, we reduce costs. So you can be a conservative that wants to save money or a progressive that wants more health care. When we invest in public education, we create a resilient economy that should be attractive to Republicans. The economic argument behind that, I think, on housing, when more people have stable housing, the economy is better. I think we can work with Republicans," Jolly said.One issue where the two candidates agree is on school choice. Both told me they support keeping universal vouchers in place.Jolly also emphasized his desire to increase transparency requirements in Florida's charter schools and increase teacher pay in public schools."Let's engage in a little bit of consumer protection here on behalf of kids and families, and say that if you're going to take a voucher as a school, you should have to provide the same services, standards and offerings and be measured by the same measuring stick that our public schools are," Jolly said.Asked whether financial records of charter schools should be public records, as they are for public schools, Donalds replied, "I think if you're talking about what parents are looking for, what they want to basically see, are the children being educated? What are the mathematical attainment scores of that school? What are the reading attainment scores of that school? And if you're talking about high school, what's the ACT scores and what's the SAT scores? I think that's the accountability and the transparency that parents are looking for in the state of Florida, because at the end of the day, they're looking to make sure that the output is where it needs to be."Donalds' wife, Erika Donalds, founded a charter school company and currently runs a nonprofit promoting school choice. "My wife is actually not in the charter school business anymore. She's actually been out of that business for a couple of years," Donalds told me. "But I just want to be clear: she will not be contracting with the state of Florida in any way, shape, or form."On data center policy, the candidates differ. Jolly said he supports a moratorium on data center construction, while Donalds believes those decisions should be left up to local governments."If a local government says no data centers, then no data centers. If they do, then where the state steps in is we make sure that utility bills, utility costs are not passed on to consumers, and we also make sure that we are going to protect water resources in our state," Donalds said.For the first time in decades, Florida voters did not get to see a gubernatorial debate for this election.Asked what he would say to Jolly had the two candidates faced one another on the debate stage, Donalds said, "I would like him to explain why and how the people of Florida are going to be able to pay for his insurance plan, because by independent analysis, his insurance plan will drive up premiums on the people of our state, and everybody will be hit with a $1,000 hurricane tax when the next time the big storm comes through," referring to the funding the sovereign wealth fund Jolly says he would like to create to cover windstorm damage for Florida homeowners. (Jolly has denied that the fund would impose a new tax.)"I'm not sure debates improve our politics at this point. I think they just platform the division and the vitriol and the ugliness," Jolly told me. "My wife says in a world of Donald Trump, I'm trying to be Ted Lasso. We have two young kids, and I want them to look back and know that Dad acted in a way that he spoke of, which was not to further devolve our politics into vitriol and ugliness and division. Debates are about who can score the greatest insult, and I just I don't think that helps."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge, 34, dies on duty
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire District confirmed that firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge, 34, died Saturday morning while on duty. Hodge joined the district on July 17, 2017, and was assigned to Station 9 in Fort Pierce.

A procession of firefighters and personnel from other agencies traveled from HCA Lawnwood Hospital to the morgue in Fort Pierce on Saturday morning. The district said it will share information about memorial arrangements and opportunities to honor Hodge’s service in coordination with his family as plans are finalized.

“His death is a profound loss to the St. Lucie County Fire District and the fire service community,” the agency said. “The District extends its heartfelt condolences to Hodge’s family, friends, and fellow firefighters during this difficult time.” The district also thanked the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Fort Pierce Police Department, Port St. Lucie Police Department, and peer support teams from Martin and Indian River counties for supporting its firefighters and helping honor Hodge.

Hodge’s younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also served with the St. Lucie County Fire District. He died on July 22, 2025, after falling ill at work at Station 3. His family said he had the flu, felt weak and was later rushed to the hospital, where he died hours later. People gathered May 30 for a cookout and balloon release to celebrate what would have been his 27th birthday.

Austin Hodge spoke about his brother’s influence at that gathering. “He was a quiet leader, and we take a lot from him. He was my younger brother, but I looked up to him in many ways to keep me poised, keep me patient. And I think that's what he's teaching everybody today.”

hero.headline: Florida approves USAA auto insurance rate cuts averaging 7% for over 498,000 policies
hero.body:
Florida Insurance Commissioner Mike Yaworsky has approved USAA Group auto insurance rate reductions averaging 7% across more than 498,000 policies statewide, according to the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation. The approvals cover several auto insurance programs, with savings varying by program.

Average rate decreases range from 0.4% to 11.2%, according to the state. USAA has its highest concentration of Florida business in Brevard, Escambia and Okaloosa counties. Average reductions in those counties are 5.8% in Brevard, 8% in Escambia and 8.4% in Okaloosa.

“The Office of Insurance Regulation is constantly reaching out to insurers to inquire about rate relief, and USAA is always stepping up to the plate and looking out for their consumers,” Yaworsky said in a release. He also encouraged other insurers to consider additional rate reductions.

Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia characterized the reductions as another sign of improvement in the state's insurance market and credited Florida's tort reforms. “These auto insurance rate decreases will help Florida families keep more of their hard-earned money in their pockets, especially our military families,” Ingoglia said.

The latest approvals follow other savings USAA provided to Florida members over the past year. Between December 2025 and July 2026, the company provided nearly $1 billion in rate reductions and direct member returns, according to the release. That total included a $500 million dividend distributed to approximately 830,000 members.

State regulators also reported that Florida's five largest auto insurance groups have a combined indicated rate change of negative 12.6% for 2026. Those companies represent 81% of the state's auto insurance market, according to the release. The state also reported that Florida's personal auto liability loss ratio was 52.5% in 2025, the lowest in the nation and Florida's lowest level in 15 years.

hero.headline: Missing 5-year-old Mayra Glory Odelus found dead in water in Fort Pierce
hero.body:
Mayra Glory Odelus, a 5-year-old girl reported missing in Fort Pierce, was found dead in a nearby body of water Saturday afternoon, according to the Fort Pierce Police Department.

“Our deepest condolences are with Mayra’s family and loved ones during this tragic time,” police said.

hero.headline: Jensen Beach High School standout Andrew Burnette gains another year at Louisiana Tech
hero.body:
Former Jensen Beach High School standout Andrew Burnette has gained another season of football at Louisiana Tech after hiring a lawyer and challenging the NCAA over his eligibility. Burnette had exhausted his eligibility after his first season at the Division I level and spent a few months working with his father at a steel mill in Detroit. A change in NCAA eligibility rules this summer opened a path for him to seek one final year on the field.

Burnette moved from Michigan around age 12 and played football in Martin County. At Jensen Beach High School, wrestling initially drew him to the school. “I wasn't zoned for that school, but I went there for wrestling originally; that was my first passion,” said Burnette. As he progressed through high school, his focus shifted toward football. He established himself on the football field but struggled to attract college recruiters. “One of my main struggles was recruitment out of high school, because I felt like our area was a little under-recruited,” he said.

He began his college career at Highland Community College in Kansas, where he played nine games and rushed for 340 yards and two touchdowns. He then transferred to Independence Junior College, where he was cut from the team. Burnette contacted Keiser University in West Palm Beach, which had offered him a chance to play while he was in high school. A coach reviewed his film and invited him to join the program. Over two years at Keiser, Burnette rushed for more than 2,300 yards and 30 touchdowns, drawing interest from Division I programs, starting with Louisiana Tech.

After his first season at Louisiana Tech, Burnette returned to Michigan to work with his father. This summer, the NCAA announced the 5-in-5 rule, allowing student-athletes to compete for up to five seasons within a continuous five-year period. Burnette hired a lawyer and went to court against the NCAA before receiving another year of eligibility. “It was amazing; I would rather play football than do anything, and for me to have this opportunity again, it's a blessing,” he said.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge, 34, dies while on duty
hero.body:
St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge, 34, died Saturday morning while on duty, the St. Lucie County Fire District said. Hodge was assigned to Station 9 in Fort Pierce and had been with the district since July 17, 2017. Firefighters and personnel from other agencies took part in a procession Saturday morning from HCA Lawnwood Hospital to the morgue in Fort Pierce. The district described his death as a significant loss for its personnel and the broader fire service community. It offered condolences to his family, friends and fellow firefighters and said memorial arrangements would be announced as plans are completed with his family.

Hodge’s death came about a year after the death of his younger brother, Jarius Hodge, who also served with the St. Lucie County Fire District. Jarius died July 22, 2025, after becoming ill while working at Station 3. His family said he had the flu and felt weak before being rushed to a hospital, where he died hours later. On May 30, people gathered for a cookout and balloon release to mark what would have been his 27th birthday. Austin Hodge reflected on his brother’s influence at that gathering: “He was a quiet leader, and we take a lot from him. He was my younger brother, but I looked up to him in many ways to keep me poised, keep me patient. And I think that's what he's teaching everybody today.”

In the hours after Austin Hodge’s death, district firefighters, Honor Guard members and public safety partners gathered to honor him and support his family and colleagues. The district thanked the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office, Fort Pierce Police Department, Port St. Lucie Police Department and peer support teams from Martin and Indian River counties. It said their assistance helped ensure Hodge was treated with dignity and respect. The district also expressed gratitude to fellow first responders and community members for their support, describing the connections among firefighters as rooted in trust, shared experiences and commitment to one another.

Condolences also came from Port St. Lucie Fire Rescue, the Fort Pierce Police Officers Association, the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office, Indian River County Emergency Services Department, Indian River County Fire Rescue, Palm Beach County Fire Rescue and Riviera Beach Fire Rescue. Another district firefighter, Connor Whitehead, 21, died May 31. The St. Lucie County Fire District has 20 fire stations and 523 firefighters, according to its website. It said information about opportunities to honor Austin Hodge’s service would be shared in coordination with his family as details are finalized.

cards.headline: Man dies after medical distress at Fort Pierce Service Plaza on Florida's Turnpike
cards.teaser: FHP said the man died at a hospital after being found unresponsive Sunday morning. Investigators do not suspect foul play.
cards.body:
A man who suffered medical distress Sunday morning at Fort Pierce Service Plaza on Florida's Turnpike died after being taken to a hospital, the Florida Highway Patrol said.

FHP units from Post 5 found the man at 5:40 a.m. He was unresponsive, was not breathing and had no pulse. He was transported to Florida Coast Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead, FHP said.

People traveling with the man said he had not been feeling well. FHP said no foul play is suspected in his death.

Lucie County Fire District spokesperson told WPBF the patient was transported to Florida Coast Medical Center in Port St. He was pronounced deceased at the hospital, FHP said. cards.headline: St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge, 34, dies on duty; served in Fort Pierce
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire District confirmed that firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge, 34, died Saturday morning while on duty. Hodge joined the district on July 17, 2017, and was assigned to Station 9 in Fort Pierce. The district said information about memorial arrangements and opportunities to honor his service will be shared in coordination with his family as plans are finalized.

A procession of firefighters and personnel from other agencies traveled from HCA Lawnwood Hospital to the morgue in Fort Pierce on Saturday morning. “His death is a profound loss to the St. Lucie County Fire District and the fire service community,” the agency said. The district thanked its firefighters, Honor Guard and public safety partners for honoring Hodge and supporting one another in the hours after his death.

Hodge’s brother, Jarius Hodge, also served with the St. Lucie County Fire District. He died on July 22, 2025, after falling ill at work at Station 3. His family said he had the flu, felt weak and was later rushed to the hospital, where he died hours later. People gathered May 30 for a cookout and balloon release to celebrate what would have been his 27th birthday. Austin Hodge described his younger brother as a quiet leader whom he looked up to for patience and poise.

The district thanked the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Fort Pierce Police Department, Port St. Lucie Police Department and peer support teams from Martin and Indian River counties for their support. Agencies offering condolences included the Fort Pierce Police Officers Association, Indian River County Sheriff's Office, Indian River County Emergency Services Department and Indian River County Fire Rescue.

hero.body:
Jensen Beach faced Fort Pierce Westwood on Friday with the District 13-4A football championship at stake, seeking its fourth district title in five years. The Falcons entered the matchup after a 51-0 victory over Legacy the previous week, a shutout highlighted by two defensive touchdowns from senior linebacker Alex Thornton. The district contest put Jensen Beach among the Treasure Coast teams playing for championship honors on a night that also brought a title-winning performance from Vero Beach. For the Falcons, the matchup with Westwood offered an opportunity to add another championship to their recent run of district success.

Thornton supplied two of the biggest plays in Jensen Beach’s win over Legacy, returning a pair of interceptions for touchdowns. His scoring returns were part of a performance in which the Falcons held their opponent scoreless while putting up 51 points. That result gave Jensen Beach momentum heading into its meeting with Fort Pierce Westwood, where the stakes shifted to the district championship. The Falcons’ pursuit of a fourth title in five years was a central storyline entering Friday’s game, following a week in which their defense contributed both points and a shutout.

Vero Beach secured the District 8-6A championship by defeating rival Treasure Coast 24-0 on Friday. The Fighting Indians’ defense kept Treasure Coast off the scoreboard, continuing its strong play late in the season. The victory stretched Vero Beach’s winning streak to six games and added a district championship to that run. Vero Beach had been pursuing a third straight district title, and the shutout against its rival continued the program’s sustained success in district competition. While Jensen Beach entered its matchup seeking another championship, Vero Beach delivered a title-clinching result with a three-touchdown margin and a clean defensive performance against Treasure Coast.

hero.headline: ACLU Letter Alleges Abuse, Medical Neglect at 'Deportation Depot' Facility
hero.body:
The ACLU and other advocacy groups have filed a letter alleging widespread abuse of detainees at the Florida immigration detention facility known as "Deportation Depot." The groups say they conducted dozens of interviews with people currently or recently detained at the facility, their loved ones, and attorneys who represent detainees there, and that those interviews point to a pattern of serious abuse.

The letter identifies seven categories of abuse: life-threatening medical neglect; lack of adequate food and clean drinking water; excessive, life-threatening heat; squalid, unsanitary, and unsafe living conditions; deprivation of necessities for physical, mental, and emotional wellbeing such as sleep, family visitation, and outdoor recreation; verbal and physical abuse and retaliation; and lack of access to the courts and to confidential communication with attorneys. On the issue of food, the letter states that detainees are not given enough nutritious food, describing portions as "extremely small, infant-sized food portions that are not filling" that lack adequate protein or nutrients. It cites cases of dramatic weight loss, including one detainee who lost 29 pounds in less than two months and another who lost 44 pounds over seven months.

On water, the letter alleges the facility does not provide adequate access to clean drinking water. It says the only water available in the dorms most of the time comes from visibly rusty fountains, and that newly arrived detainees are warned by others not to drink from them because many people have gotten sick doing so. One former detainee named Ryan said he and others would try to drink as much water as possible from the cafeteria during their brief mealtimes because it was the only source of clean water. He said that in the dorms, "you had no alternative sometimes than just to kind of take your chances with the water," describing it as having "a very strong metallic taste" that made his stomach feel like "something was kicking and punching" it once it settled.

ACLU attorney Amy Godshall, who wrote the letter, said the facility appears designed to strip detainees of basic dignity. "It's very much a cruel facility that's designed to deny people every aspect of humanity and decency and dignity, and is designed to make people physically weak, mentally weak, and just pressured to agree to the point where they agree to self deportation," she said. The letter argues this pressure may be intentional, stating there is evidence of a deliberate effort to make detention conditions unbearable so that people give up their legal rights and accept removal, adding that whether or not the conditions are intentional, they are punitive and unconstitutional. Ryan said he was approached by guards on three or four separate occasions and asked to sign forms consenting to his own deportation. "The question that a lot of us had is, well, if we were deportable, then why would we have to sign this document to make us deportable?" he said.

When Alligator Alcatraz shut down over the summer, it didn't end Florida's involvement in immigration detention. There's a second state-run facility that's been open for a year in a former prison about 50 minutes west of Jacksonville. Because its location is less controversial than the Everglades, it's flown largely under the radar. But now, detainees are speaking up about the alleged horrors inside what state officials have dubbed 'Deportation Depot.' 'It's insane. There's no other word [to describe the situation] than insanity. Just how bad these conditions were,' said a man who asked that we hide his face and refer to him by his middle name, Ryan. He fears being publicly identified could jeopardize his still-pending immigration case. 'I'm happy to be here, and I'm grateful, and obviously I'm gonna do everything I can to complete my immigration journey, and hopefully I can put this behind me,' Ryan said. I learned from the American Civil Liberties Union and confirmed through federal court records and local news reports that Ryan was detained by immigration authorities in late February and sent to the Baker Correctional Institution in Sanderson, where he spent four months. hero.headline: Jensen Beach's Andrew Burnette wins legal fight for fifth year, returns to Louisiana Tech
hero.body:
Jensen Beach native Andrew Burnette has won back a fifth season of college football eligibility after taking his case to court against the NCAA, and he is now back on the field at Louisiana Tech. Burnette moved to Martin County from Michigan around age 12 and went on to star at Jensen Beach High School, where he originally enrolled to wrestle before football took over as his main focus. "I wasn't zoned for that school, but I went there for wrestling originally; that was my first passion," Burnette said. "Moving through high school, I knew football was what I wanted to do."

Despite his success at Jensen Beach High School, Burnette said he did not draw much interest from college recruiters, a common experience for Treasure Coast football players. "One of my main struggles was recruitment out of high school, because I felt like our area was a little under-recruited," he said. He chose to play at Highland Community College in Kansas, where he rushed for 340 yards and two touchdowns in nine games, but still failed to attract bigger programs. He then transferred to Independence Junior College, a school featured on the Netflix series Last Chance U, but was cut from that team.

Burnette reached out to Keiser University in West Palm Beach, reminding the coaching staff that they had offered him a spot back in high school. "I spoke with the coach there and told him, 'You guys offered me in high school,' and he said, 'I don't really remember. Send me your film.' He saw my film and said, 'Hey, bring it,'" Burnette said. Over two seasons at Keiser, he rushed for more than 2,300 yards and scored 30 touchdowns, numbers that finally caught the attention of Division I programs, including Louisiana Tech. He played his first Division I season there last year, but his NCAA eligibility ran out under the old four-year limit.

Rather than walk away from the game, Burnette called his father and took a job working alongside him at a steel mill in Detroit. "I called my dad and told him, 'Hey, I need to do something. I can't just sit here,' so I went and worked with my dad in Michigan," he said. This summer the NCAA adopted a new 5-in-5 rule, allowing athletes to compete in up to five seasons within a continuous five-year window. Burnette hired a lawyer and took his case to court against the NCAA, which granted him a final season of eligibility. He is now back on the field at Louisiana Tech. "It was amazing; I would rather play football than do anything, and for me to have this opportunity again, it's a blessing," Burnette said.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County Firefighter Austin Hodge Dies on Duty, Brother Died in 2025
hero.teaser: St. Lucie County Fire District firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge died on duty Saturday, just over a year after his brother Jarius died while serving in the same role. The Hodge family had publicly pushed for accountability after Jarius's 2025 death at a Port St. Lucie hospital.
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Fire District firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge died while on duty Saturday, Oct. 24, more than a year after his younger brother Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic, died at age 26. The district announced Austin's line-of-duty death Saturday, calling it a profound loss to the department and the fire service community. Austin Hodge had joined the district on July 17, 2017, and served the community for more than nine years, most recently assigned to Station 9. Neighboring Indian River County Fire Rescue also shared condolences following his unexpected death Saturday morning. The circumstances surrounding Austin's death have not been released, and the fire district asked the public to respect his family's privacy as they grieve.

Jarius Hodge died on July 22, 2025, after becoming ill with the flu he contracted from a patient at work earlier that month. Austin said his brother had been healthy before getting sick and alleged that medical staff made critical errors in his treatment, including taking three attempts to intubate him.

The brothers shared a close bond built around their shared career in firefighting. "This was my best friend, my twin," Austin said of Jarius in the earlier interview. "We had the same hairstyle." He described his brother as someone who loved going to work and loved working alongside him. "He loved going to work, loved working beside me. I loved working beside him," Austin said. "He always pushed me to keep going. He was someone who loved his family, his community and his country."

After Jarius's death, Austin spoke publicly about Florida's medical malpractice laws, arguing that restrictions on who can pursue certain wrongful-death claims prevented his family from seeking legal accountability. "This is unjust, and it's been going on for too long," Austin said. He stressed that the family wanted accountability, not money. "For me personally, for my family, this has nothing to do with any type of dollar," he said. "We just want those physicians to be held accountable." The St. Lucie County Fire District said it will share information about memorial arrangements and ways to honor Austin Hodge's service once details are finalized in coordination with his family.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Police Arrest Newspaper Delivery Driver in NW California Boulevard Hit-and-Run
cards.teaser: A geofence warrant and matching vehicle fasteners helped detectives crack the two-week case, but police say they are still looking for a second vehicle.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police have arrested a 60-year-old newspaper delivery driver in connection with the Oct. 9 hit-and-run crash that left a 63-year-old resident critically injured on NW California Boulevard. Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said detectives arrested Eric Saint Aude on Oct. 22 and charged him with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury.

The crash happened shortly before 1 a.m. on NW California Boulevard just south of the intersection with NW University Boulevard. The victim was found unconscious in the road with severe head injuries and remains in critical condition at HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce. Niemczyk said Aude was working as a newspaper delivery driver and was on his way to pick up newspapers when the crash happened.

Investigators spent two weeks reviewing video, physical evidence and other leads before making an arrest. Niemczyk said a geofence warrant seeking cellphone location data from the crash area and time produced a lead showing Aude's phone had pinged off cell towers there at the time of the crash, pointing detectives toward Aude and vehicles registered to him. Detectives then located and examined his vehicle, which had damage to the front bumper and hood consistent with striking a pedestrian, along with presumptive positive results for blood that require further testing. Police also recovered pieces of the vehicle's inner fender-well fasteners at the scene and found that several matching fasteners were missing from Aude's vehicle.
